figures.alt: Master Cherry pauses over the talking piece of wood.

paragraphs: “Once upon a time…”
“There was a king!” my young readers will say at once.
“No, children, you’ve got it wrong. Once upon a time there was a piece of wood.”
It was not fine, expensive wood, but an ordinary piece from a woodpile, the kind people put in stoves and fireplaces in winter to light a fire and warm their rooms.

I don’t know how it happened, but the fact is that one day this piece of wood ended up in the workshop of an old carpenter whose name was Master Antonio, though everyone called him Master Cherry, because the tip of his nose was always shiny and dark red, like a ripe cherry.
As soon as Master Cherry saw that piece of wood, he was delighted; and rubbing his hands together with joy, he muttered quietly:
“This wood has come just in time; I’ll use it to make a leg for a little table.”

No sooner said than done, he picked up his sharp axe to start stripping off the bark and cutting the wood into shape; but just as he was about to bring the axe down for the first time, his arm stopped in mid-air, because he heard a tiny, tiny voice begging:
“Don’t hit me so hard!”
￼ch01
Just imagine how that dear old Master Cherry felt!

He looked around the room in confusion to see where that tiny voice could have come from, and he saw no one! He looked under the workbench, and no one was there: he looked inside a cupboard that was always kept shut, and no one was there; he looked in the basket of wood shavings and sawdust, and no one was there; he opened the workshop door to look out into the street as well, and no one was there. Well, then…?
“I see,” he said, laughing and scratching his wig, “I must have imagined that tiny voice. Let’s get back to work.”
And picking up the axe again, he brought it down on the piece of wood with a huge blow.
“Ow! You hurt me!” cried the same tiny voice in pain.
This time Master Cherry froze, his eyes bulging with fear, his mouth wide open and his tongue hanging down to his chin, like a carved face on a fountain.
As soon as he could speak again, he began to say, shaking and stammering with fear:

“But where can that tiny voice that said ‘ow’ have come from…? Yet there isn’t a soul here. Could this piece of wood have learned to cry and complain like a child? I can’t believe it. Here is the wood; it’s a piece of firewood like any other, and if you put it on the fire, it would boil a pot of beans… Well, then? Could someone be hiding inside it? If someone is hiding there, so much the worse for him. I’ll soon sort him out!”
And as he said this, he grabbed the poor piece of wood with both hands and began to bang it against the walls of the room without mercy.
Then he listened to hear whether any tiny voice was complaining. He waited two minutes, and nothing; five minutes, and nothing; ten minutes, and nothing!
“I see,” he said, forcing a laugh and messing up his wig, “I must have imagined that tiny voice that said ‘ow’! Let’s get back to work.”
And because he was so frightened, he tried humming a little tune to give himself some courage.
Meanwhile, putting the axe aside, he picked up his wood plane to shave the piece of wood smooth; but as he moved the tool back and forth over it, he heard the same tiny voice laughing and saying:
“Stop! You’re tickling me all over!”
This time poor Master Cherry fell down as if lightning had struck him. When he opened his eyes again, he found himself sitting on the floor.
His face looked completely changed, and even the tip of his nose, which was nearly always dark red, had turned blue with fright.
chapters.title: How Master Cherry the carpenter found a piece of wood that cried and laughed like a child.

paragraphs: Just then there was a knock at the door.
“Come in,” said the carpenter, without the strength to stand up.

Then a lively little old man called Geppetto came into the workshop; but whenever the children nearby wanted to make him furious, they called him Polendina, or Little Corn Porridge, because of his yellow wig, which looked very much like corn porridge.
Geppetto had a terrible temper. Just try calling him Polendina! He would turn into a wild beast at once, and there was no holding him back.
“Good morning, Master Antonio,” said Geppetto. “What are you doing down there on the floor?”
“Teaching the ants to count.”
“I hope it does you some good.”
“What brought you here, my friend Geppetto?”
“My legs. You see, Master Antonio, I’ve come to ask you a favour.”
“Here I am, ready to help,” replied the carpenter, rising onto his knees.
“This morning an idea dropped into my head.”
“Let’s hear it.”

“I thought I’d make myself a fine wooden puppet: but a wonderful puppet that can dance, fence with a sword, and turn somersaults. With this puppet I want to travel the world, to earn myself a crust of bread and a glass of wine: what do you think?”
“Bravo, Polendina!” cried the same tiny voice, whose hiding place nobody could work out.
Hearing himself called Polendina, Geppetto turned as red as a pepper with anger, and turning towards the carpenter, he said furiously:
“Why are you insulting me?”
“Who’s insulting you?”
“You called me Polendina!”
“It wasn’t me.”
“Oh, so I suppose it was me! I say it was you.”
“No!”
“Yes!”
“No!”
“Yes!”
And growing angrier and angrier, they went from words to blows, and grabbing hold of each other, they scratched, bit, and knocked each other about.
When the fight was over, Master Antonio found Geppetto’s yellow wig in his hands, and Geppetto discovered the carpenter’s grey-streaked wig in his mouth.
“Give me back my wig!” shouted Master Antonio.
“And you give me back mine, and let’s make peace.”
The two little old men, after each had taken back his own wig, shook hands and swore to remain good friends for the rest of their lives.
“Well then, my friend Geppetto,” said the carpenter to show that they had made peace, “what is the favour you want from me?”
“I’d like a bit of wood to make my puppet; will you give me some?”

Master Antonio, delighted, went straight to fetch from the workbench the piece of wood that had given him so many frights. But just as he was about to hand it to his friend, the piece of wood gave a sudden jerk, and slipping violently out of his hands, struck poor Geppetto hard on his thin, dried-up shins.
“Ah! Is this your polite way of giving things away, Master Antonio? You’ve almost crippled me!…”
“I swear it wasn’t me!”
“Then I suppose it was me!…”
“It’s all this wood’s fault…”
“I know it was the wood: but you threw it at my legs!”
“I didn’t throw it at you!”
“Liar!”
“Geppetto, don’t insult me: or I’ll call you Polendina!…”
“Donkey!”
“Polendina!”
“Ass!”
“Polendina!”
“Ugly little monkey!”
“Polendina!”
Hearing himself called Polendina for the third time, Geppetto went blind with rage, threw himself at the carpenter, and they gave each other a terrible beating.

When the battle was over, Master Antonio had two more scratches on his nose, and the other man had two fewer buttons on his jacket. Having settled their scores in this way, they shook hands and swore to remain good friends for the rest of their lives.
Then Geppetto took his fine piece of wood, and after thanking Master Antonio, limped home.
chapters.title: Master Cherry gives the piece of wood to his friend Geppetto, who takes it to make himself a wonderful puppet that can dance, fence with a sword, and turn somersaults.

paragraphs: Geppetto’s home was a little room on the ground floor, which got its light from under a staircase. The furniture could not have been simpler: a poor chair, a rather bad bed, and a little table that was falling apart. On the far wall you could see a fireplace with a fire burning in it; but the fire was painted, and beside it was a painted pot, boiling away merrily and sending up a cloud of smoke that looked like real smoke.
As soon as he got home, Geppetto picked up his tools and began to carve and make his puppet.

“What shall I call him?” he said to himself. “I’ll call him Pinocchio. That name will bring him luck. I once knew a whole family of Pinocchios: Pinocchio the father, Pinocchia the mother, and Pinocchi the children, and they all got along well. The richest of them begged for a living.”
Once he had found a name for his puppet, he got down to work properly, and first made the hair, then the forehead, then the eyes.
With the eyes finished, just imagine his surprise when he noticed that the eyes were moving and staring straight at him.
Geppetto, finding those two wooden eyes looking at him, almost took offence, and said in a hurt voice:
“You nasty wooden eyes, why are you staring at me?”
No one answered.
Then, after the eyes, he made the nose; but as soon as the nose was made, it began to grow: and it grew, grew, grew, until in a few minutes it was an enormous nose that seemed to have no end.
Poor Geppetto worked hard to cut it back; but the more he cut and shortened it, the longer that cheeky nose grew.
After the nose he made the mouth.
The mouth was not even finished before it began to laugh and make fun of him.
“Stop laughing!” said Geppetto, offended; but he might as well have spoken to a wall.
“Stop laughing, I tell you!” he shouted in a threatening voice.
Then the mouth stopped laughing, but stuck its tongue right out.
Geppetto, so as not to spoil his work, pretended not to notice and carried on. After the mouth he made the chin, then the neck, then the shoulders, the stomach, the arms, and the hands.
As soon as the hands were finished, Geppetto felt his wig being pulled off his head. He looked up, and what did he see? He saw his yellow wig in the puppet’s hand.
“Pinocchio!… Give me back my wig at once!”
And Pinocchio, instead of giving back the wig, put it on his own head, almost disappearing underneath it.
At this rude, mocking behaviour, Geppetto grew sadder and more miserable than he had ever been in his life: and turning to Pinocchio, he said:
“You little rascal of a son! You aren’t even finished yet, and already you’re showing no respect for your father! Bad, my boy, bad!”
And he wiped away a tear.
The legs and feet still had to be made.
When Geppetto had finished making the feet, he felt a kick land on the tip of his nose.
“I deserve it,” he said to himself. “I should have thought of this before! It’s too late now!”
Then he took the puppet under the arms and set him down on the floor of the room, to make him walk.
Pinocchio’s legs were stiff and he could not move, and Geppetto led him by the hand to teach him to put one foot in front of the other.
Once his legs had loosened up, Pinocchio began to walk on his own and run around the room; until, darting through the door, he leapt into the street and ran away.

And poor Geppetto ran after him without being able to catch him, because that rascal Pinocchio bounded along like a hare, and his wooden feet clattering on the street’s paving stones made as much noise as twenty pairs of farmers’ wooden clogs.

“Catch him! Catch him!” shouted Geppetto; but the people in the street, seeing this wooden puppet running like a racehorse, stopped to stare in wonder, and laughed and laughed and laughed more than you can imagine.

At last, luckily, a policeman came along, and hearing all that noise and thinking it must be a young horse that had escaped its owner, he bravely planted himself in the middle of the street with his legs apart, firmly meaning to stop it and prevent any worse accidents.
But when Pinocchio saw the policeman in the distance, blocking the whole street, he tried to slip between his legs by surprise, and failed.

The policeman, without moving an inch, neatly caught him by the nose (it was an absurdly long nose, which seemed made especially for policemen to grab) and handed him straight back to Geppetto, who wanted to give his ears a good tug at once to teach him a lesson. But imagine how he felt when he looked for the ears and could not find them: and do you know why? Because, in his hurry to carve him, he had forgotten to make them.
So he took him by the back of the neck, and as he led him back, he said, shaking his head threateningly:
“We’re going straight home. Once we’re home, you can be sure we’ll settle our accounts!”
At these words, Pinocchio threw himself on the ground and refused to walk any farther. Meanwhile, curious people and people with nothing to do began to stop nearby and gather in a crowd.
One said one thing, another something else.
“Poor puppet!” some said. “He’s right not to want to go home! Who knows how that brute Geppetto would beat him!…”
And others added spitefully:
“That Geppetto looks like a decent man! But he’s a real bully with children! If they leave that poor puppet in his hands, he’s quite capable of tearing him to pieces!”

In short, they said and did so much that the policeman set Pinocchio free and took poor Geppetto to prison. Having no words ready to defend himself, he wept like a little calf, and as he headed towards the prison, he stammered between sobs:
“Wretched boy! And to think I worked so hard to make him a good puppet! But it serves me right! I should have thought of it before!…”
What happened next is a story so strange that you can hardly believe it, and I shall tell it to you in the following chapters.
chapters.title: Back home, Geppetto starts making the puppet at once and names him Pinocchio. The puppet’s first naughty tricks.

paragraphs: Well, children, I’ll tell you that while poor Geppetto was being taken to prison through no fault of his own, that rascal Pinocchio, free of the policeman’s clutches, was racing across the fields to get home sooner; and in his wild hurry he leapt over very high banks, thorn hedges, and ditches full of water, just as a little goat or a young hare chased by hunters might have done.

When he reached the house, he found the street door half open. He pushed it, went inside, and as soon as he had slid the bolt firmly across, he threw himself down on the floor with a great sigh of happiness.
But that happiness did not last long, because he heard someone in the room go:
“Chirp-chirp-chirp!”
“Who’s calling me?” said Pinocchio, frightened.
“I am!”
Pinocchio turned and saw a large cricket slowly climbing up and up the wall.
“Tell me, Cricket, who are you?”
“I am the Talking Cricket, and I have lived in this room for more than a hundred years.”
“But today this room is mine,” said the puppet, “and if you really want to do me a favour, leave at once, without even looking back.”
“I won’t leave here,” answered the Cricket, “until I have told you a great truth.”
“Tell me, and be quick about it.”

“Trouble awaits children who turn against their parents and leave their father’s home just because they feel like it. They will never do well in this world; and sooner or later they will be bitterly sorry.”

“Sing away, my dear Cricket, as much as you please: but I know I want to leave here tomorrow at dawn, because if I stay here, the same thing will happen to me as happens to all the other children, which means they’ll send me to school, and whether I like it or not I’ll have to study; and between you and me, I don’t want to study at all, and I have more fun chasing butterflies and climbing trees to take baby birds from their nests.”
“You poor little fool!… But don’t you know that if you carry on like that, you’ll grow up to be a proper donkey, and everyone will make fun of you?”
“Be quiet, you nasty cricket, always warning of trouble!” shouted Pinocchio.
But the cricket, who was patient and wise, instead of taking offence at this rudeness, went on in the same tone:
“And if you don’t like going to school, why don’t you at least learn a trade, so you can honestly earn a piece of bread?”
“Shall I tell you?” replied Pinocchio, who was beginning to lose patience. “Of all the jobs in the world, there’s only one that really suits me.”
“And what job would that be?”
“Eating, drinking, sleeping, having fun, and wandering about doing nothing from morning till night.”
“Just so you know,” said the Talking Cricket as calmly as ever, “people who do that job almost always end up in hospital or prison.”
“Watch out, you nasty cricket, always warning of trouble!… If I lose my temper, you’ll be sorry!”
“Poor Pinocchio: I really feel sorry for you!…”
“Why do you feel sorry for me?”
“Because you’re a puppet and, worse still, because you have a wooden head.”
At these last words, Pinocchio jumped up in a fury, and taking a wooden hammer from the workbench, hurled it at the Talking Cricket.

Perhaps he did not even think he would hit him; but sadly he struck him right on the head, so that the poor Cricket barely had the breath to go chirp-chirp-chirp, and then stayed there stone dead, stuck to the wall.
chapters.title: The story of Pinocchio and the Talking Cricket, which shows how naughty children hate being corrected by those who know more than they do.

paragraphs: Meanwhile it began to grow dark, and Pinocchio, remembering that he had eaten nothing, felt a little ache in his stomach that was very much like an appetite.
But a child’s appetite moves fast, and sure enough, after a few minutes his appetite became hunger, and in the blink of an eye that hunger became a wolf’s hunger, a hunger you could cut with a knife.

Poor Pinocchio ran straight to the fireplace, where a pot was boiling, and reached to lift the lid and see what was inside: but the pot was painted on the wall. Imagine how he felt. His nose, which was already long, grew at least another four fingers’ width.

Then he began running around the room and searching every little box and cupboard for a bit of bread, even dry bread, a little crust, a bone the dog had left, some mouldy corn porridge, a fishbone, a cherry stone, in short anything to chew: but he found nothing, absolutely nothing, nothing at all.

And meanwhile his hunger grew and kept on growing: and poor Pinocchio had no comfort except yawning, and his yawns were so long that sometimes his mouth stretched as far as his ears. And after yawning he spat, and felt his stomach fading away.
Then, crying in despair, he said:
“The Talking Cricket was right. I was wrong to turn against my dad and run away from home… If my dad were here now, I wouldn’t be dying of yawns! Oh! What a terrible illness hunger is!”
Just then he thought he saw something round and white in the rubbish heap that looked exactly like a hen’s egg. In a single instant he leapt and pounced on it. It really was an egg.

It is impossible to describe the puppet’s joy: you must imagine it for yourself. Hardly believing it was not a dream, he turned the egg over in his hands, and touched it and kissed it, and as he kissed it he said:

“And now how shall I cook it? Shall I make an omelette?… No, better to cook it in a dish!… Or wouldn’t it taste better if I fried it in a pan? Or what if I soft-boiled it so I could drink it? No, the quickest way of all is to cook it in a dish or a little pan: I’m too eager to eat it!”

No sooner said than done, he put a little pan over a pot full of glowing coals: he put a little water into the pan instead of oil or butter: and when the water began to steam, crack!… he broke the eggshell and went to tip the egg into it.
But instead of the white and yolk, out popped a cheerful, very polite chick, which made a fine bow and said:
“A thousand thanks, Mr Pinocchio, for saving me the trouble of breaking the shell! Goodbye, keep well, and give everyone at home my best wishes!”
Having said this, it spread its wings, shot through the open window, and flew away out of sight.

The poor puppet stayed there as if under a spell, with staring eyes, an open mouth, and the eggshells in his hands. But when he recovered from his first shock, he began to cry, scream, and stamp his feet in despair, and as he cried he said:
“And the Talking Cricket was right after all! If I hadn’t run away from home and my dad were here, I wouldn’t be dying of hunger now. Oh! What a terrible illness hunger is!…”

And because his stomach kept growling worse than ever, and he did not know how to quiet it, he decided to leave the house and run to the nearby village, hoping to find some kind person who would give him a little bread.
chapters.title: Pinocchio is hungry and finds an egg to make an omelette; but just at the best moment, the omelette flies out of the window.

paragraphs: As it happened, it was a night straight out of hell. The thunder crashed and crashed, lightning flashed as if the sky were on fire, and a wild, cold wind, whistling furiously and raising an enormous cloud of dust, made all the trees in the countryside creak and groan.

Pinocchio was terribly afraid of thunder and lightning: but hunger was stronger than fear: so he pulled the door to, and setting off at a run, reached the village in a hundred leaps, with his tongue hanging out and panting like a hunting dog.
But he found everything dark and deserted. The shops were shut; the house doors shut, the windows shut, and not even a dog in the street. It seemed like a village of the dead.
Then Pinocchio, overcome by despair and hunger, grabbed a house bell and began ringing it without stopping, saying to himself:
“Someone will come to the window.”
Sure enough, an old man in a nightcap appeared and shouted angrily:
“What do you want at this hour?”
“Would you please give me a little bread?”
“Wait there, I’ll be right back,” replied the little old man, thinking he was dealing with one of those reckless boys who enjoy ringing doorbells at night to bother decent people sleeping peacefully.
Half a minute later the window opened again, and the same little old man’s voice shouted to Pinocchio:
“Come underneath and hold out your hat.”
Pinocchio, who did not yet have a hat, came closer and felt an enormous basinful of water pour down over him, watering him from head to foot as if he were a pot of drooping geraniums.

He went home as wet as a little chick and worn out with tiredness and hunger: and because he no longer had the strength to stand, he sat down, resting his soaking, muddy feet on a pot full of glowing coals.
And there he fell asleep; and as he slept, his feet, which were made of wood, caught fire and slowly, slowly burned black and turned to ash.
And Pinocchio went on sleeping and snoring, as if his feet belonged to someone else. At last, as day was breaking, he woke because someone had knocked at the door.
“Who is it?” he asked, yawning and rubbing his eyes.
“It’s me!” answered a voice.
That voice was Geppetto’s.
chapters.title: Pinocchio falls asleep with his feet on the pot of coals, and next morning wakes up with his feet burned away.

paragraphs: Poor Pinocchio, whose eyes were still full of sleep, had not yet noticed that his feet had burned right away: so as soon as he heard his father’s voice, he shot down from the stool to run and draw back the bolt; but instead, after two or three wobbles, he fell flat on his face on the floor.
And when he hit the floor, he made the same noise as a bag of wooden spoons falling from the fifth floor.
“Open the door!” Geppetto was shouting from the street.
“Dad, I can’t…” answered the puppet, crying and rolling on the floor.
“Why can’t you?”
“Because my feet have been eaten.”
“And who ate them?”
“The cat,” said Pinocchio, seeing the cat amusing itself by batting some wood shavings about with its front paws.
“Open the door, I tell you!” Geppetto repeated. “Or when I get inside, I’ll give you something to blame on the cat!”
“I can’t stand up, believe me. Oh, poor me! Poor me, I’ll have to walk on my knees for the rest of my life.”
Geppetto, thinking all this whining was another of the puppet’s naughty tricks, decided to put an end to it; and climbing up the wall, he came into the house through the window.

At first he was ready to scold and punish him; but then, when he saw his Pinocchio stretched on the floor and truly without feet, his heart softened; and taking him straight into his arms, he began to kiss and stroke him and shower him with loving words, and with great tears rolling down his cheeks, he said between sobs:
“My little Pinocchio! How did you burn your feet?”

“I don’t know, Dad, but believe me, it was a night from hell, and I’ll remember it as long as I live. It thundered and flashed and I was terribly hungry, and then the Talking Cricket said to me, ‘Serves you right: you’ve been naughty and you deserve it,’ and I said, ‘Watch out, Cricket!…’ and he said, ‘You’re a puppet and you have a wooden head,’ and I threw a hammer handle at him, and he died, but it was his fault, because I didn’t want to kill him, and the proof is that I put a little pan over the glowing coals, but the chick jumped out and said, ‘Goodbye… and give everyone at home my best wishes.’ And I kept getting hungrier, which is why that little old man in the nightcap looked out of the window and said, ‘Come underneath and hold out your hat,’ and with that basinful of water over my head, because there’s no shame in asking for a little bread, is there? I went straight home, and because I was still so hungry, I put my feet on the pot of coals to dry myself, and you came back, and I found them burned away, and now I’m still hungry and I haven’t got my feet any more! Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!…”
And poor Pinocchio began crying and howling so loudly that he could be heard five kilometres away.
Geppetto, who had understood only one thing from that tangled speech, namely that the puppet felt he was dying of hunger, took three pears from his pocket, and offering them to him, said:
“These three pears were my breakfast: but I’m happy to give them to you. Eat them, and enjoy them.”
“If you want me to eat them, please peel them for me.”

“Peel them?” replied Geppetto in surprise. “I would never have thought, my boy, that you were such a fussy eater and so hard to please. That’s bad! In this world, from childhood on, we must get used to eating whatever there is, because we never know what might happen to us. All sorts of things can happen!…”
“You may be right,” added Pinocchio, “but I’ll never eat fruit that hasn’t been peeled. I can’t stand the skins.”
And good-hearted Geppetto took out a little knife, and gathering all his patience, peeled the three pears and put all the skins on a corner of the table.
When Pinocchio had eaten the first pear in two bites, he went to throw the core away; but Geppetto caught his arm, saying:
“Don’t throw it away: anything in this world can come in useful.”
“But I certainly won’t eat the core!…” cried the puppet, turning on him like a snake.
“Who knows! All sorts of things can happen!…” repeated Geppetto without getting angry.
The result was that the three cores, instead of being thrown out of the window, were placed on the corner of the table beside the skins.
Having eaten, or rather gobbled up, the three pears, Pinocchio gave a very long yawn and said with a whine:
“I’m still hungry!”
“But I have nothing more to give you, my boy.”
“Really nothing, nothing at all?”
“I only have these pear skins and cores.”
“Oh well!” said Pinocchio. “If there’s nothing else, I’ll eat a skin.”

And he began to chew. At first he pulled a face: but then, one after another, he polished off all the skins in a flash; and after the skins, the cores as well, and when he had finished everything, he happily patted his stomach and said with delight:
“Now I really do feel good!”

“You see, then,” Geppetto pointed out, “I was right when I said you mustn’t get used to being too fussy or too picky about your food. My dear boy, you never know what might happen to you in this world. All sorts of things can happen!…”
chapters.title: Geppetto comes home and gives the puppet the breakfast the poor man had brought for himself.

paragraphs: As soon as the puppet’s hunger was gone, he began grumbling and crying because he wanted a new pair of feet.
But Geppetto, to punish him for his naughty behaviour, let him cry and fret for half a day; then he said:
“And why should I make you new feet? So I can watch you run away from home again?”
“I promise,” said the puppet, sobbing, “that from today on I’ll be good…”
“All children,” replied Geppetto, “say that when they want something.”
“I promise I’ll go to school, study, and make you proud…”
“All children tell the same story when they want something.”
“But I’m not like other children! I’m better than all of them, and I always tell the truth. I promise, Dad, I’ll learn a trade, and I’ll be your comfort and the stick you lean on in your old age.”

Geppetto, who, though he was putting on a fierce face, had eyes full of tears and a heart aching with love at the sight of his poor Pinocchio in that sorry state, said nothing more: but taking his tools and two little pieces of well-dried wood, he set to work with all his might.
And in less than an hour the feet were finished: two slim little feet, neat and strong, as if a brilliant artist had shaped them.
Then Geppetto said to the puppet:
“Close your eyes and go to sleep!”

And Pinocchio closed his eyes and pretended to sleep. And while he was pretending, Geppetto used a little glue melted in an eggshell to stick the two feet into place, and he stuck them on so well that you could not even see the join.
As soon as the puppet realised he had feet, he jumped down from the table where he was lying and began kicking his legs and turning somersaults over and over, as if he had gone mad with happiness.
“To repay you for everything you’ve done for me,” Pinocchio told his dad, “I want to go to school at once.”
“Good boy.”
“But to go to school, I need some clothes.”

Geppetto, who was poor and did not have even a centesimo in his pocket, made him a little suit out of flower-patterned paper, a pair of shoes out of tree bark, and a little cap out of the soft inside of a loaf of bread.
Pinocchio ran straight to look at himself in a basin of water and was so pleased with himself that he said, showing off proudly:
“I look just like a gentleman!”
“You do,” replied Geppetto, “because, remember, it isn’t fine clothes that make a gentleman, but clean clothes.”
“By the way,” added the puppet, “I’m still missing something for school: in fact, I’m missing the most important thing of all.”
“Which is?”
“I haven’t got an ABC book.”
“You’re right: but how can we get one?”
“It’s very easy: you go to a bookseller and buy it.”
“And the money?”
“I haven’t got any.”
“Neither have I,” added the good old man, looking sad.
And Pinocchio, though he was a very cheerful boy, looked sad too: because everyone understands poverty when it is real poverty, even children.
“Oh well!” cried Geppetto suddenly, getting to his feet; and slipping on his old thick cloth coat, all patches and repairs, he ran out of the house.
He came back shortly afterwards: and when he returned, he had the ABC book for his son in his hand, but his coat was gone. The poor man had only his shirt on, and outside it was snowing.
“What about your coat, Dad?”
“I sold it.”
“Why did you sell it?”
“Because it made me hot.”
Pinocchio understood this answer at once, and unable to hold back the rush of love in his good heart, he threw his arms around Geppetto’s neck and began kissing him all over his face.
chapters.title: Geppetto makes Pinocchio new feet and sells his own coat to buy him an ABC book.

paragraphs: Once the snow had stopped, Pinocchio set off along the road to school with his fine new ABC book under his arm: and as he went, his little head filled with a thousand plans and a thousand castles in the air, each more splendid than the last.
And talking to himself, he said:

“Today at school I’ll learn to read straight away: tomorrow I’ll learn to write, and the day after tomorrow I’ll learn to do sums. Then, with my skills, I’ll earn lots of money, and with the first money that comes into my pocket, I’ll get Dad a fine cloth coat at once. But why am I saying cloth? I’ll have it made entirely of silver and gold, with diamond buttons. And the poor man really deserves it; because, after all, to buy me books and let me learn, he was left in just his shirt… in this cold! Only dads can give up so much!…”
As he was saying this, full of feeling, he thought he heard music in the distance, pipes and the beats of a big drum: peep-peep-peep, peep-peep-peep, boom, boom, boom, boom.
He stopped and listened. The sounds came from the far end of a very long side road leading to a little village built on the seashore.
“What can that music be? What a pity I have to go to school, otherwise…”
And he stood there, unable to decide. Still, he had to make a choice: either school or listening to the pipes.
“Today I’ll go and hear the pipes, and tomorrow I’ll go to school. There’s always time for school,” the rascal said at last with a shrug.

No sooner said than done, he turned down the side road and began running as fast as he could. The farther he ran, the more clearly he heard the pipes and the thumps of the big drum: peep-peep-peep, peep-peep-peep, peep-peep-peep, boom, boom, boom, boom.
And there he was in the middle of a square full of people crowding around a large booth made of wood and canvas painted in a thousand colours.
“What’s that booth?” Pinocchio asked, turning to a boy from the village who was standing nearby.
“Read the sign, and you’ll know.”
“I’d gladly read it, but as it happens, today I can’t read.”
“You great ox! Then I’ll read it for you. You should know that the sign, in letters as red as fire, says: GRAND PUPPET THEATRE…”
“Has the play been going on long?”
“It’s starting now.”
“And how much does it cost to get in?”
“Four soldi.”
Pinocchio, burning with curiosity, forgot all self-control and said without shame to the boy he was talking to:
“Would you lend me four soldi until tomorrow?”
“I’d gladly lend them to you,” the other replied mockingly, “but as it happens, today I can’t.”
“I’ll sell you my jacket for four soldi,” the puppet said then.
“What would I do with a jacket made of flowery paper? If rain falls on it, you can’t get it off your back.”
“Do you want to buy my shoes?”
“They’re good for lighting a fire.”
“How much will you give me for my cap?”
“What a fine thing to buy! A cap made from the inside of a loaf! The mice might come and eat it right off my head!”
Pinocchio was on edge. He was about to make his last offer, but he could not find the courage: he hesitated, wavered, and suffered. At last he said:
“Will you give me four soldi for this new ABC book?”
“I’m a child, and I don’t buy things from children,” answered the little boy, who had more sense than he did.
“I’ll take the ABC book for four soldi,” called a second-hand clothes seller who had been there during the conversation.
And the book was sold on the spot. And to think that poor Geppetto had stayed at home, shivering in his shirtsleeves, to buy his son the ABC book!
chapters.title: Pinocchio sells his ABC book to go and see the puppet theatre.

paragraphs: When Pinocchio entered the little puppet theatre, something happened that caused almost a revolution.
You must know that the curtain was up and the play had already begun.
On the stage, Harlequin and Punchinello were quarrelling and, as usual, threatening at any moment to exchange a load of slaps and blows with sticks.

The audience, watching closely, was laughing itself sick at the argument between the two puppets, who waved their arms and called each other every rude name so convincingly that they might have been two thinking creatures, two real people in this world.
When all at once, out of the blue, Harlequin stops acting, turns towards the audience, points to someone at the back, and begins shouting dramatically:
“Gods of the heavens! Am I dreaming or awake? Why, that’s Pinocchio over there!…”
“It really is Pinocchio!” cries Punchinello.
“It’s him!” shrieks Miss Rosaura, peeping out at the back of the stage.
“It’s Pinocchio! It’s Pinocchio!” all the puppets shouted together, leaping out from the wings.
“It’s Pinocchio! It’s our brother Pinocchio! Hooray for Pinocchio!…”
“Pinocchio, come up here to me!” cries Harlequin. “Come into the arms of your wooden brothers!”

At this loving invitation, Pinocchio gives a leap from the back of the theatre to the best seats; then with another leap he jumps from the best seats onto the head of the orchestra conductor, and from there springs onto the stage.

It is impossible to imagine the hugs, neck squeezes, friendly pinches, and head bumps of true, heartfelt brotherhood that Pinocchio received in the great tangle of actors and actresses from that wooden theatre company.
It was a touching sight, no doubt about it: but the audience, seeing that the play was going no further, grew impatient and began to shout, “We want the play! We want the play!”

All wasted breath, because instead of going on with the performance, the puppets made twice as much noise, and lifting Pinocchio onto their shoulders, carried him in triumph to the lights at the front of the stage.

Then out came the puppet master, a huge man so ugly that the sight of him alone was frightening. He had a great beard as black as an ink scribble, and so long that it reached from his chin to the ground: it is enough to say that when he walked, he stepped on it. His mouth was as wide as an oven, his eyes looked like two red glass lanterns lit from behind; and in his hands he cracked a thick whip made of snakes and fox tails twisted together.
At the puppet master’s unexpected appearance, everyone fell silent: no one made another sound. You could have heard a fly pass. Those poor puppets, male and female, trembled like leaves.
“Why have you come to turn my theatre upside down?” the puppet master asked Pinocchio in the booming voice of an ogre with a terrible head cold.
“Please believe me, most honoured sir, it wasn’t my fault!…”
“That’s enough! Tonight we’ll settle our accounts.”

Sure enough, when the play was over, the puppet master went into the kitchen, where he had prepared a fine sheep for his supper, turning slowly on a roasting spit. And because he had run out of wood to finish cooking and browning it, he called Harlequin and Punchinello and said:
“Bring me that puppet you’ll find hanging on the nail. He looks like a puppet made of very dry wood, and I’m sure that if I throw him on the fire, he’ll give me a splendid blaze for the roast.”

At first Harlequin and Punchinello hesitated; but frightened by a fierce look from their master, they obeyed: and then they returned to the kitchen carrying poor Pinocchio in their arms, while he wriggled like an eel out of water and screamed desperately, “Dad, save me! I don’t want to die, no, I don’t want to die!…”
chapters.title: The puppets recognise their brother Pinocchio and give him a wonderful welcome; but just at the best moment the puppet master Fire-Eater appears, and Pinocchio is in danger of a terrible end.

paragraphs: The puppet master Fire-Eater (for that was his name) looked frightening, I won’t deny it, especially with that huge black beard covering his whole chest and all his legs like an apron; but deep down he was not a bad man. The proof is that when he saw poor Pinocchio brought before him, struggling in every direction and shouting, “I don’t want to die, I don’t want to die!” he immediately began to feel moved and sorry for him; and after holding out for quite a while, he could stand it no longer and let out an extremely loud sneeze.
At that sneeze, Harlequin, who until then had been sad and bent over like a weeping willow, brightened up, and leaning towards Pinocchio, whispered softly:
“Good news, brother! The puppet master sneezed, and that means he feels sorry for you, and now you’re safe.”

For you must know that while other men, when they feel sorry for someone, cry or at least pretend to wipe their eyes, Fire-Eater had a habit of sneezing whenever his heart was truly touched. It was as good a way as any to let others know how tender his heart was.
After sneezing, the puppet master, still acting gruff, shouted at Pinocchio:
“Stop crying! Your whining has given me an ache deep in my stomach… I feel a sharp pain that almost… achoo, achoo!” And he sneezed twice more.
“Bless you!” said Pinocchio.
“Thank you. And are your dad and your mum still alive?” asked Fire-Eater.
“My dad is; I never knew my mum.”
“Who knows how sad your old father would be if I had you thrown onto those burning coals now. Poor old man! I feel sorry for him… achoo, achoo, achoo!” And he sneezed three more times.
“Bless you!” said Pinocchio.

“Thank you. Still, you must feel sorry for me too, because as you can see, I have no more wood to finish roasting that sheep, and to tell the truth, you would have been very useful to me just now! But now I’ve felt sorry for you, and I must put up with it. Instead of you, I’ll burn one of the puppets in my company under the spit. Guards!”
At this order, two wooden guards appeared at once, very tall and very thin, with wide two-pointed hats on their heads and drawn swords in their hands.
Then the puppet master said to them in a rough, rattling voice:
“Grab that Harlequin over there, tie him up tight, and throw him onto the fire to burn. I want my sheep properly roasted!”
Imagine poor Harlequin! He was so frightened that his legs folded beneath him and he fell face down on the floor.
At this heartbreaking sight, Pinocchio threw himself at the puppet master’s feet, and crying floods of tears that soaked every hair of that very long beard, began to say in a pleading voice:
“Have mercy, Mr Fire-Eater!…”
“There are no misters here!” snapped the puppet master.
“Have mercy, noble knight!…”
“There are no knights here!”
“Have mercy, Commander!”
“There are no commanders here!”
“Have mercy, Your Excellency!…”
On hearing himself called Your Excellency, the puppet master immediately pursed his lips, and suddenly becoming kinder and easier to deal with, said to Pinocchio:
“Well, what do you want from me?”
“I’m begging you to spare poor Harlequin!…”
“There’s no question of sparing him. If I’ve spared you, I must have him put on the fire, because I want my sheep properly roasted.”

“In that case,” cried Pinocchio proudly, standing up and throwing away his bread cap, “in that case I know what I must do. Come on, guards! Tie me up and throw me into those flames. No, it isn’t right for poor Harlequin, my true friend, to die for me!”
These words, spoken loudly and bravely, made all the puppets watching the scene cry. Even the guards, though made of wood, wept like two newborn lambs.

At first Fire-Eater stayed as hard and still as a block of ice: but then, little by little, he too began to feel moved and sneeze. And after four or five sneezes, he opened his arms lovingly and said to Pinocchio:
“You are a very good boy! Come here and give me a kiss.”
Pinocchio ran straight over, and climbing like a squirrel up the puppet master’s beard, planted a lovely kiss on the tip of his nose.
“So you’ll spare me?” asked poor Harlequin in a tiny voice that could hardly be heard.
“I’ll spare you!” answered Fire-Eater; then he added, sighing and shaking his head:
“Oh well! Tonight I’ll put up with eating my sheep half raw: but next time, pity whoever’s turn it is!…”
At the news that Harlequin had been spared, all the puppets ran onto the stage, and lighting the lamps and chandeliers as if for a grand celebration, began to jump and dance.
Dawn came, and they were still dancing.
chapters.title: Fire-Eater sneezes and forgives Pinocchio, who then saves his friend Harlequin from death.

paragraphs: The next day Fire-Eater called Pinocchio aside and asked him:
“What is your father’s name?”
“Geppetto.”
“And what does he do for a living?”
“He’s poor.”
“Does he earn much?”

“He earns just enough never to have a centesimo in his pocket. Just think, to buy my school ABC book he had to sell the only coat he had: a coat so full of patches and repairs that it was one great wound.”
“Poor fellow! I almost feel sorry for him. Here are five gold coins. Go straight and take them to him, and give him my very best wishes.”

Pinocchio, as you can easily imagine, thanked the puppet master a thousand times: he hugged every puppet in the company one by one, even the guards; and beside himself with happiness, he set off on his journey home.

But he had not gone even half a kilometre when he met a Fox who was lame in one foot and a Cat who was blind in both eyes, making their way along the road, helping each other like good companions in misfortune. The Fox, who was lame, walked leaning on the Cat: and the Cat, who was blind, let the Fox guide him.
“Good morning, Pinocchio,” said the Fox, greeting him politely.
“How do you know my name?” asked the puppet.
“I know your dad well.”
“Where have you seen him?”
“I saw him yesterday at his front door.”
“And what was he doing?”
“He was in his shirtsleeves, shivering with cold.”
“Poor Dad! But, God willing, from today on he won’t shiver any more!”
“Why?”
“Because I’ve become a very rich gentleman.”
“You, a rich gentleman?” said the Fox, and burst into a rude, mocking laugh: and the Cat laughed too, but to hide it he combed his whiskers with his front paws.
“There’s nothing to laugh at,” cried Pinocchio, offended. “I’m truly sorry to make your mouths water, but these, if you know anything about it, are five beautiful gold coins.”
And he took out the coins Fire-Eater had given him.

At the pleasant sound of those coins, the Fox, without meaning to, stretched the leg that had seemed stiff and twisted, and the Cat opened both eyes wide, like two green lanterns; but then he shut them again so quickly that Pinocchio noticed nothing.
“And now,” the Fox asked, “what are you going to do with those coins?”
“First of all,” answered the puppet, “I’m going to buy Dad a fine new coat, all gold and silver, with diamond buttons: and then I’ll buy an ABC book for myself.”
“For yourself?”
“Yes, because I want to go to school and really get down to studying.”
“Look at me!” said the Fox. “Because of my foolish love of studying, I lost the use of a leg.”
“Look at me!” said the Cat. “Because of my foolish love of studying, I lost the sight in both my eyes.”
Just then a white Blackbird, perched on the hedge beside the road, gave its usual call and said:
“Pinocchio, don’t listen to advice from bad companions, or you’ll be sorry!”
Poor Blackbird, if only he had never said it! The Cat gave a great leap, pounced on him, and before he even had time to say “ow”, ate him in one bite, feathers and all.
After eating him and cleaning his mouth, he shut his eyes again and went back to pretending to be blind.
“Poor Blackbird!” Pinocchio said to the Cat. “Why did you treat him so badly?”
“I did it to teach him a lesson. Next time he’ll know not to butt into other people’s conversations.”
They had gone more than halfway when the Fox suddenly stopped and said to the puppet:
“Would you like to double your gold coins?”
“What do you mean?”
“Would you like to turn five miserable gold coins into a hundred, a thousand, two thousand?”
“If only! But how?”
“It’s very easy. Instead of going home, you should come with us.”
“And where do you want to take me?”
“To the Land of Barn Owls.”
Pinocchio thought for a moment, then said firmly:

“No, I don’t want to come. I’m close to home now, and I want to go home, where my dad is waiting for me. Who knows how the poor old man sighed yesterday when I didn’t come back. I really have been a bad son, and the Talking Cricket was right when he said, ‘Disobedient children cannot do well in this world.’ And I’ve learned that the hard way, because so many bad things have happened to me, and even last night at Fire-Eater’s I was in danger… Brrr! I get shivers just thinking about it!”
“So,” said the Fox, “you really want to go home? Then go ahead, and so much the worse for you.”
“So much the worse for you!” repeated the Cat.
“Think carefully, Pinocchio, because you’re kicking good fortune away.”
“Good fortune!” repeated the Cat.
“Your five gold coins would have become two thousand overnight.”
“Two thousand!” repeated the Cat.
“But how can they possibly become so many?” asked Pinocchio, his mouth hanging open in amazement.

“I’ll explain right away,” said the Fox. “You must know that in the Land of Barn Owls there is a blessed field that everyone calls the Field of Miracles. You make a little hole in this field and put in, for example, one gold coin. Then you cover the hole with a little earth: you water it with two buckets of water from the fountain, sprinkle a pinch of salt on top, and in the evening you go peacefully to bed. Meanwhile, during the night, the gold coin sprouts and flowers, and when you get up the next morning and return to the field, what do you find? You find a fine tree loaded with as many gold coins as a fine ear of wheat has grains in June.”
“So then,” said Pinocchio, more and more amazed, “if I buried my five gold coins in that field, how many gold coins would I find there the next morning?”

“It’s a very easy sum,” answered the Fox, “a sum you can count on your fingers. Suppose each gold coin gives you a bunch of five hundred gold coins: multiply five hundred by five, and the next morning you’ll have two thousand five hundred bright, jingling gold coins in your pocket.”
“Oh, how wonderful!” cried Pinocchio, dancing with joy. “As soon as I’ve picked those gold coins, I’ll take two thousand for myself and give the other five hundred to you two as a present.”
“A present for us?” cried the Fox, angry and saying he was offended. “God forbid!”
“God forbid!” repeated the Cat.
“We,” the Fox went on, “don’t work for dirty profit: we work to make other people rich.”
“Other people!” repeated the Cat.
“What good people!” Pinocchio thought to himself: and forgetting on the spot his dad, the new coat, the ABC book, and all his good plans, he said to the Fox and the Cat:
“Let’s go at once, I’m coming with you.”
chapters.title: The puppet master Fire-Eater gives Pinocchio five gold coins to take to his dad Geppetto; but instead Pinocchio lets the Fox and the Cat trick him and goes off with them.

paragraphs: They walked and walked and walked, and at last, as evening fell, they reached the Red Crayfish Inn, dead tired.
“Let’s stop here a while,” said the Fox, “just to have a bite to eat and rest for a few hours. Then we’ll set off again at midnight, so we can be at the Field of Miracles at dawn tomorrow.”
They went into the inn and all three sat down at the table: but none of them had any appetite.

The poor Cat, whose stomach was terribly upset, could manage nothing but thirty-five red mullet in tomato sauce and four helpings of tripe with Parmesan cheese: and because he thought the tripe did not have enough flavour, he asked three more times for butter and grated cheese!

The Fox would gladly have nibbled something too: but since the doctor had put him on a very strict diet, he had to make do with a simple hare in sweet-and-sour sauce, with a very light side dish of fat young hens and young cockerels just learning to crow. After the hare, he ordered a little stew of partridges, grey partridges, rabbits, frogs, lizards and sweet grapes to tempt his appetite; and then he wanted nothing more.
Food made him feel so sick, he said, that he could not bring anything near his mouth.

Pinocchio ate less than anyone. He asked for a piece of walnut and a crust of bread, and left everything on his plate. The poor child, whose thoughts were fixed on the Field of Miracles, had already given himself a stomachache in advance from gold coins.
When they had finished supper, the Fox said to the innkeeper:

“Give me two good rooms, one for Mr Pinocchio and another for me and my companion. We’ll have a little nap before we leave. But remember, we want to be woken at midnight to carry on with our journey.”
“Yes, sir,” replied the innkeeper, and he winked at the Fox and the Cat, as if to say, “I see what’s going on, and we understand each other!”

As soon as Pinocchio got into bed, he fell asleep at once and began to dream. And in his dream he seemed to be in the middle of a field, and the field was full of little trees loaded with bunches, and the bunches were loaded with gold coins which, swaying in the wind, went chink, chink, chink, almost as if they were saying, “Whoever wants us, come and get us.” But just as Pinocchio reached the best part, just as he stretched out his hand to gather handfuls of all those lovely coins and put them in his pocket, he was suddenly woken by three very loud knocks on his bedroom door.
It was the innkeeper, coming to tell him that midnight had struck.
“And are my companions ready?” the puppet asked him.
“Ready? They left two hours ago.”
“Why were they in such a hurry?”
“Because the Cat received a message saying that his eldest kitten, who had painful sores on his feet from the cold, was in danger of dying.”
“And did they pay for supper?”
“What do you think? Those are far too well-mannered gentlemen to insult you like that, sir.”
“What a pity! That insult would have pleased me very much!” said Pinocchio, scratching his head. Then he asked:
“And where did those good friends say they would wait for me?”
“At the Field of Miracles, tomorrow morning at daybreak.”
Pinocchio paid one gold coin for his own supper and his companions’ suppers, and then set off.

But you might say he set off feeling his way, because outside the inn it was so dark that you could not see a thing. In the countryside all around, not a leaf could be heard stirring. Only a few ugly night birds, crossing the road from one hedge to another, brushed their wings against Pinocchio’s nose, making him jump back in fright and shout, “Who’s there?” and the echo from the nearby hills repeated in the distance, “Who’s there? Who’s there? Who’s there?”
Meanwhile, as he walked, he saw a little creature on the trunk of a tree, shining with a pale, dull light, like a nightlight inside a lamp of thin porcelain.
“Who are you?” Pinocchio asked it.
“I am the ghost of the Talking Cricket,” replied the little creature in a very faint voice that seemed to come from the world of the dead.
“What do you want with me?” said the puppet.
“I want to give you some advice. Turn back and take the four gold coins you have left to your poor father, who is crying and in despair because he hasn’t seen you again.”
“Tomorrow my father will be a rich gentleman, because these four gold coins will become two thousand.”
“My boy, don’t trust people who promise to make you rich overnight. Usually they are either mad or cheats! Listen to me, turn back.”
“But I want to go on.”
“It’s late!”
“I want to go on.”
“The night is dark…”
“I want to go on.”
“The road is dangerous…”
“I want to go on.”
“Remember that children who insist on doing whatever they please will regret it sooner or later.”
“The same old stories. Good night, Cricket.”
“Good night, Pinocchio, and may heaven keep you safe from the night damp and the murderers.”
As soon as he had said these last words, the Talking Cricket suddenly went out, like a light blown out with a breath, and the road was darker than before.
chapters.title: The Red Crayfish Inn.

paragraphs: “Really,” the puppet said to himself as he set off again, “how unlucky we poor children are! Everyone scolds us, everyone warns us, everyone gives us advice. If you let them talk, they would all get it into their heads that they were our fathers and our teachers; all of them; even Talking Crickets. Just look: because I wouldn’t listen to that tiresome Cricket, who knows how many terrible things he thinks will happen to me! I’m even supposed to meet murderers! Luckily, I don’t believe in murderers, and I never have. I think fathers invented murderers just to frighten children who want to go out at night. And even if I did meet them here on the road, would I be afraid of them? Not a chance, I would go right up to them and shout, ‘Mr Murderers, what do you want with me? Remember, I’m not someone to mess with! So be off about your business, and keep quiet!’ Hearing a serious speech like that, those poor murderers, I can just see them, would run away like the wind. And if they were so rude that they refused to run away, then I would run away, and that would settle it…”
But Pinocchio could not finish his thoughts, because just then he seemed to hear a very faint rustling of leaves behind him.
He turned to look, and in the darkness he saw two horrible black figures, wrapped from head to foot in coal sacks, running after him with little leaps and on tiptoe, as if they were two ghosts.
“There they really are!” he said to himself: and not knowing where to hide the four gold coins, he hid them in his mouth, right under his tongue.
Then he tried to run away. But before he had taken his first step, he felt himself grabbed by the arms and heard two horrible, hollow voices saying:
“Your money or your life!”

Pinocchio, unable to answer in words because of the coins in his mouth, made a thousand bows and a thousand gestures to explain to the two hooded figures, whose eyes alone showed through holes in the sacks, that he was a poor puppet and did not even have a fake coin in his pocket.
“Come on! Less talk, and hand over the money!” the two robbers shouted threateningly.
And the puppet made a sign with his head and hands, as if to say, “I haven’t got any.”
“Hand over the money or you’re dead,” said the taller murderer.
“Dead!” repeated the other.
“And after we kill you, we’ll kill your father too!”
“Your father too!”
“No, no, no, not my poor father!” Pinocchio cried desperately: but as he shouted, the gold coins jingled in his mouth.
“Ah, you rascal! So you’ve hidden the money under your tongue? Spit it out at once!”
But Pinocchio stood firm.
“Ah! Pretending you can’t hear? Just wait, we’ll make you spit it out!”

And one of them grabbed the puppet by the tip of his nose and the other took hold of his chin, and they began pulling roughly, one this way and the other that way, to force his mouth open: but nothing worked. The puppet’s mouth seemed nailed and bolted shut.

Then the shorter murderer pulled out a huge knife and tried to push it between his lips like a lever or a chisel: but Pinocchio, quick as lightning, sank his teeth into his hand, and after biting it clean off, spat it out, and imagine his surprise when he realised that instead of a hand he had spat a cat’s paw onto the ground.

Encouraged by this first victory, he forced himself out of the murderers’ clutches, jumped over the roadside hedge and began to flee across the countryside. And the murderers ran after him like two dogs chasing a hare: and the one who had lost a paw ran on just one leg, and no one has ever discovered how he did it.

After running fifteen kilometres, Pinocchio could go no farther. Then, seeing that he was lost, he climbed up the trunk of a very tall pine tree and sat among its top branches. The murderers tried to climb up too, but halfway up the trunk they slipped, and falling back to the ground, scraped the skin off their hands and feet.

They did not give up for all that: instead, they gathered a bundle of dry wood at the foot of the pine and set fire to it. In no time, the pine began to burn and blaze like a candle in the wind. Pinocchio, seeing the flames climbing higher and not wanting to end up like a roast pigeon, took a great leap from the treetop and set off running again through the fields and vineyards. And the murderers were behind him, always behind him, never growing tired.

Meanwhile, day was beginning to break, and he suddenly found his way blocked by a wide, very deep ditch, full of dirty water the colour of milky coffee. What could he do? “One, two, three!” shouted the puppet, and taking a long run-up, he jumped to the other side. And the murderers jumped too, but they had not judged the distance properly, and splash!… they fell right into the middle of the ditch. Pinocchio, hearing the thud and the splash of water, shouted, laughing as he kept on running:
“Enjoy your swim, Mr Murderers.”

He was already imagining that they had drowned, when instead, turning to look, he saw that they were both running after him, still wrapped in their sacks and pouring water like two baskets with holes in the bottom.
chapters.title: Having ignored the Talking Cricket’s good advice, Pinocchio runs into the murderers.

paragraphs: Then the puppet lost heart and was just about to throw himself on the ground and give up, when, looking around, he saw a little house as white as snow gleaming in the distance among the dark green trees.
“If I had enough breath to reach that house, perhaps I would be safe!” he said to himself.
And without wasting a minute, he began running through the wood again at full speed. And the murderers were still behind him.
After a desperate run of almost two hours, he finally reached the little house’s door, completely out of breath, and knocked.
No one answered.
He knocked again, harder, because he could hear the footsteps and heavy, breathless panting of his pursuers coming closer.
The same silence.

Seeing that knocking did no good, he began desperately kicking the door and banging his head against it. Then a beautiful little Girl appeared at the window, with blue hair and a face as white as a wax figure, her eyes closed and her hands crossed over her chest, and without moving her lips at all, she said in a tiny voice that seemed to come from the world of the dead:
“There is no one in this house; they are all dead.”
“At least you can open the door for me!” cried Pinocchio, weeping and begging.
“I am dead too.”
“Dead? Then what are you doing there at the window?”
“I am waiting for the coffin to come and take me away.”
As soon as she had said this, the Girl disappeared and the window closed without a sound.
“Oh, beautiful little Girl with blue hair,” cried Pinocchio, “please open the door! Have pity on a poor boy being chased by murd—”
But he could not finish the word, because he felt himself seized by the neck, and the same two horrible voices growled threateningly:
“Now you won’t get away from us again!”
The puppet, seeing death flash before his eyes, began trembling so hard that the joints of his wooden legs and the four gold coins hidden under his tongue rattled as he shook.
“Well?” the murderers asked him. “Will you open your mouth, yes or no? Ah! You won’t answer? Just wait: this time we’ll open it for you!”
And drawing two very long knives as sharp as razors, swish and swish… they stabbed him twice in the lower back.
But luckily the puppet was made of very hard wood, so the blades broke into a thousand pieces, and the murderers were left staring at each other with the knife handles in their hands.
“I see,” one of them said then, “we must hang him. Let’s hang him!”
“Let’s hang him,” repeated the other.
No sooner said than done, they tied his hands behind his back and, putting a rope loop that pulled tight around his throat, hung him dangling from a branch of a huge tree called the Great Oak.
Then they sat there on the grass, waiting for the puppet to give his last kick: but after three hours the puppet’s eyes were still open, his mouth was still shut, and he was kicking harder than ever.
At last, tired of waiting, they turned to Pinocchio and said with nasty laughs:
“Goodbye until tomorrow. When we come back here tomorrow, we hope you’ll be kind enough to let us find you properly dead, with your mouth wide open.”
And they went away.

Meanwhile, a fierce north wind had risen, blowing and roaring angrily, tossing the poor hanging puppet from side to side and making him swing wildly like the clapper inside a bell ringing for a celebration. And that swinging caused him sharp bursts of pain, and the rope loop, tightening more and more around his throat, took his breath away.
Little by little his eyes grew dim; and although he felt death coming closer, he still kept hoping that at any moment some kind soul would arrive to help him.
But when, after waiting and waiting, he saw that no one was coming, no one at all, he remembered his poor father… and, almost dying, he stammered:
“Oh, Father! If only you were here!”
And he had no breath left to say anything more. He closed his eyes, opened his mouth, stretched out his legs and, with one great shudder, hung there as if stiff with cold.
chapters.title: The murderers chase Pinocchio; and after catching him, they hang him from a branch of the Great Oak.

paragraphs: While poor Pinocchio, whom the murderers had hanged from a branch of the Great Oak, now seemed more dead than alive, the beautiful blue-haired Girl appeared at the window again, and taking pity on the unhappy creature who, hanging by his neck, was dancing in the blasts of the north wind, she clapped her hands three times, making three little sounds.
At this signal there was a great beating of wings rushing through the air, and a large Falcon landed on the windowsill.

“What are your orders, my kind Fairy?” said the Falcon, lowering his beak in a bow; for you should know that the blue-haired Girl was, after all, none other than a very good Fairy who had lived near that wood for more than a thousand years.
“Do you see that puppet hanging from a branch of the Great Oak?”
“I see him.”
“Well then: fly there at once; use your very strong beak to break the knot that holds him in the air, and lay him gently on the grass at the foot of the Oak.”
The Falcon flew away, and two minutes later he returned, saying:
“What you ordered is done.”
“And how did you find him? Alive or dead?”
“He looked dead, but he cannot be quite dead yet, because as soon as I loosened the rope loop around his throat, he gave a sigh and stammered quietly, ‘Now I feel better!’”
Then the Fairy clapped her hands twice, making two little sounds, and a magnificent Poodle appeared, walking upright on his hind legs exactly like a man.

The Poodle was dressed in a coachman’s finest uniform. On his head he wore a little three-cornered hat trimmed with gold, a blond wig with curls falling down his neck, a chocolate-coloured coat with diamond buttons and two large pockets for the bones his mistress gave him at dinner, short trousers of deep red velvet, silk stockings, low-cut shoes, and behind him something like an umbrella cover, made entirely of blue satin, to put his tail inside when it began to rain.

“Come on, good boy, Medoro!” the Fairy said to the Poodle. “Have the finest carriage in my stable harnessed at once, and take the road to the wood. When you reach the Great Oak, you will find a poor half-dead puppet lying on the grass. Pick him up gently, lay him flat on the carriage cushions and bring him here to me. Do you understand?”
To show that he understood, the Poodle wagged the blue satin cover behind him three or four times, and set off like a racehorse.

A little later, a beautiful little sky-coloured carriage came out of the stable, padded all over with canary feathers and lined inside with whipped cream and custard with sponge biscuits. The little carriage was pulled by a hundred pairs of white mice, and the Poodle, sitting on the driver’s seat, cracked his whip right and left, like a driver afraid he was running late.

Less than a quarter of an hour had passed when the little carriage returned, and the Fairy, who was waiting at the door, took the poor puppet in her arms and carried him into a little room with mother-of-pearl walls, then sent at once for the most famous doctors in the neighbourhood.
And the doctors arrived at once, one after another: that is, a Raven, a Little Owl and a Talking Cricket.

“I would like you gentlemen to tell me,” said the Fairy, speaking to the three doctors gathered around Pinocchio’s bed, “I would like you gentlemen to tell me whether this unfortunate puppet is alive or dead!”
At this invitation, the Raven stepped forward first and felt Pinocchio’s pulse; then he felt his nose, then his little toes: and after feeling very carefully, he spoke these solemn words:
“In my opinion, the puppet is quite dead: but if, unfortunately, he were not dead, that would be a sure sign that he is still alive!”

“I am sorry,” said the Little Owl, “to have to disagree with the Raven, my famous friend and fellow doctor; in my opinion, on the contrary, the puppet is still alive; but if, unfortunately, he were not alive, that would be a sign that he is truly dead.”
“And have you nothing to say?” the Fairy asked the Talking Cricket.
“I say that when a careful doctor does not know what he is talking about, the best thing he can do is keep quiet. Besides, that puppet’s face is not new to me: I have known him for a long time!”
Pinocchio, who until then had stayed as still as a real piece of wood, gave a sudden shudder that shook the whole bed.
“That puppet,” the Talking Cricket went on, “is a first-class rascal…”
Pinocchio opened his eyes and closed them again at once.
“He is a naughty boy, a lazy fellow, a wanderer…”
Pinocchio hid his face under the sheets.
“That puppet is a disobedient son who will make his poor father die of a broken heart!”

At this point, a muffled sound of crying and sobbing could be heard in the room. Imagine everyone’s surprise when, lifting the sheets a little, they discovered that the one crying and sobbing was Pinocchio.
“When a dead person cries, it is a sign that he is getting better,” said the Raven solemnly.
“I am sorry to disagree with my famous friend and fellow doctor,” added the Little Owl, “but in my opinion, when a dead person cries, it is a sign that he is sorry to die.”
chapters.title: The beautiful blue-haired Girl has the puppet brought in: she puts him to bed and calls three doctors to find out whether he is alive or dead.

paragraphs: As soon as the three doctors had left the room, the Fairy went over to Pinocchio and, after touching his forehead, realised that he had a terribly high fever.
Then she dissolved a certain white powder in half a glass of water and, offering it to the puppet, said kindly:
“Drink this, and in a few days you’ll be well.”
Pinocchio looked at the glass, twisted his mouth a little, and then asked in a whining voice:
“Is it sweet or bitter?”
“It’s bitter, but it will do you good.”
“If it’s bitter, I don’t want it.”
“Listen to me: drink it.”
“I don’t like bitter things.”
“Drink it: and when you’ve drunk it, I’ll give you a little ball of sugar to take away the taste.”
“Where’s the sugar ball?”
“Here it is,” said the Fairy, taking it out of a golden sugar bowl.
“I want the sugar ball first, and then I’ll drink that nasty bitter water…”
“Do you promise?”
“Yes…”
The Fairy gave him the sugar ball, and Pinocchio, after crunching it up and swallowing it in an instant, said, licking his lips:
“Wouldn’t it be lovely if sugar were medicine too! I’d take it every day.”
“Now keep your promise and drink these few drops of water, which will make you well.”
Pinocchio reluctantly took the glass and stuck the tip of his nose into it: then he brought it up to his mouth: then he stuck his nose into it again: finally he said:
“It’s too bitter! Too bitter! I can’t drink it.”
“How can you say that when you haven’t even tasted it?”
“I can imagine it! I could tell by the smell. I want another sugar ball first… and then I’ll drink it!”
Then the Fairy, with all the patience of a good mother, put a little more sugar in his mouth; and afterwards she offered him the glass again.
“I can’t drink it like this!” said the puppet, making a thousand faces.
“Why?”
“Because that pillow down there on my feet is bothering me.”
The Fairy took the pillow away.
“It’s no use! I still can’t drink it.”
“What else is bothering you?”
“The bedroom door is bothering me, because it’s half open.”
The Fairy went and closed the bedroom door.
“Anyway,” cried Pinocchio, bursting into tears, “I won’t drink that nasty bitter water, no, no, no!”
“My boy, you’ll regret it…”
“I don’t care…”
“You are very ill.”
“I don’t care…”
“The fever will send you to the other world in a few hours…”
“I don’t care…”
“Aren’t you afraid of death?”
“Not at all! I’d rather die than drink that nasty medicine.”
At this point, the bedroom door flew open and four rabbits as black as ink came in, carrying a little coffin on their shoulders.
“What do you want with me?” cried Pinocchio, sitting up in bed in terror.
“We’ve come to take you away,” replied the largest rabbit.
“Take me away? But I’m not dead yet!”
“Not yet: but you have only a few moments left to live, since you refused to drink the medicine that would have cured your fever!”
“Oh, my Fairy, my Fairy!” the puppet began to scream. “Give me that glass at once… Hurry, please, because I don’t want to die, no… I don’t want to die.”
And taking the glass in both hands, he emptied it in one gulp.
“Oh well!” said the rabbits. “This time we’ve made the trip for nothing.” And lifting the little coffin onto their shoulders again, they left the room grumbling and muttering under their breath.

The fact is that a few minutes later, Pinocchio jumped out of bed, completely well; for you should know that wooden puppets have the special advantage of rarely falling ill and getting better very quickly.
And the Fairy, seeing him running and tumbling around the room, as lively and cheerful as a young cockerel just learning to crow, said:
“So my medicine really did you good?”
“Good? It brought me back to life!”
“Then why did you make me beg you so much to drink it?”
“It’s because we children are all like that! We’re more afraid of medicine than of illness.”
“Shame on you! Children should know that good medicine taken in time can save them from a serious illness and perhaps even from death…”
“Oh! But next time I won’t make you beg so much! I’ll remember those black rabbits with the coffin on their shoulders… and then I’ll take the glass straight away and down it goes…”
“Now come here to me and tell me how you ended up in the murderers’ hands.”

“What happened was that Fire-Eater the puppet-master gave me five gold coins and said, ‘Here, take them to your father!’ and instead I met a Fox and a Cat on the road, two very decent people, who said, ‘Would you like those coins to become a thousand or two thousand? Come with us, and we’ll take you to the Field of Miracles.’ And I said, ‘Let’s go’; and they said, ‘Let’s stop here at the Red Crayfish Inn, and after midnight we’ll set off again.’ And when I woke up, they weren’t there any more because they’d left. Then I started walking in the night, and it was so dark you wouldn’t believe it, so I met two murderers on the road inside coal sacks, and they said, ‘Hand over the money’; and I said, ‘I haven’t got any’; because I’d hidden the gold coins in my mouth, and one of the murderers tried to put his hands in my mouth, and I bit his hand off and then spat it out, but instead of a hand I spat out a cat’s paw. And the murderers chased me, and I ran and ran until they caught up with me, and they tied me by the neck to a tree in this wood, saying, ‘Tomorrow we’ll come back here, and then you’ll be dead with your mouth open, and we’ll take away the gold coins you’ve hidden under your tongue.’”
“And where have you put the four coins now?” the Fairy asked him.
“I’ve lost them!” replied Pinocchio; but he was telling a lie, because they were really in his pocket.
As soon as he told the lie, his nose, which was already long, immediately grew two finger-widths longer.
“And where did you lose them?”
“In the wood nearby.”
At this second lie, his nose kept growing.
“If you lost them in the nearby wood,” said the Fairy, “we’ll look for them and find them: because everything lost in the nearby wood is always found again.”
“Ah! Now I remember properly,” replied the puppet, getting mixed up, “I haven’t lost the four coins, but without noticing, I swallowed them while I was drinking your medicine.”

At this third lie, his nose grew so amazingly long that poor Pinocchio could no longer turn in any direction. If he turned this way, he hit his nose against the bed or the windowpanes, if he turned that way, he hit it against the walls or the bedroom door, if he raised his head a little higher, he risked poking the Fairy in the eye.
And the Fairy looked at him and laughed.
“Why are you laughing?” the puppet asked her, very confused and worried about his nose, which was growing before his eyes.
“I’m laughing at the lie you told.”
“How do you know I told a lie?”
“Lies, my boy, are easy to spot, because there are two kinds: there are lies with short legs, and lies with long noses: yours happens to be one of those with a long nose.”
Pinocchio, not knowing where to hide for shame, tried to run out of the room, but he could not. His nose had grown so long that it would no longer fit through the doorway.
chapters.title: Pinocchio eats the sugar but will not take his medicine; when he sees the gravediggers coming to take him away, he takes it. Then he tells a lie, and his nose grows as punishment.

paragraphs: As you can imagine, the Fairy let the puppet cry and howl for a good half-hour over his nose, which no longer fitted through the bedroom door: and she did this to teach him a firm lesson and cure him of the nasty habit of telling lies, the nastiest habit a child can have. But when she saw his face changed and his eyes bulging with despair, she took pity on him and clapped her hands, and at that signal a thousand large birds called Woodpeckers flew through the window into the room, and, landing all over Pinocchio’s nose, they pecked and pecked at it until, in a few minutes, that huge, ridiculous nose was back to its normal size.
“How kind you are, my Fairy,” said the puppet, wiping his eyes, “and how much I love you!”
“I love you too,” replied the Fairy, “and if you want to stay with me, you will be my little brother and I will be your kind little sister…”
“I’d love to stay… but what about my poor father?”
“I’ve thought of everything. Your father has already been told: and before nightfall he will be here.”
“Really?” cried Pinocchio, jumping for joy. “Then, my dear Fairy, if you don’t mind, I’d like to go and meet him! I can’t wait to kiss that poor old man who has suffered so much because of me!”
“Go ahead, but take care not to get lost. Take the path through the wood, and I’m sure you’ll meet him.”

Pinocchio set off: and as soon as he entered the wood, he began running like a deer. But when he reached a certain spot, almost opposite the Great Oak, he stopped, because he thought he had heard people among the branches. And there on the road appeared, guess who?… the Fox and the Cat, the two travelling companions with whom he had eaten supper at the Red Crayfish Inn.
“Here is our dear Pinocchio!” cried the Fox, hugging and kissing him. “How come you’re here?”
“How come you’re here?” repeated the Cat.
“It’s a long story,” said the puppet, “and I’ll tell you when there’s time. But you should know that the other night, when you left me alone at the inn, I met murderers on the road…”
“Murderers? Oh, our poor friend! And what did they want?”
“They wanted to steal my gold coins.”
“Villains!” said the Fox.
“Terrible villains!” repeated the Cat.
“But I began to run away,” the puppet went on, “and they kept chasing me: until they caught me and hanged me from a branch of that oak…”
And Pinocchio pointed to the Great Oak, which stood just a few steps away.
“Could anything be worse?” said the Fox. “What a world we are forced to live in! Where can honest folk like us find a safe place?”
While they were talking like this, Pinocchio noticed that the Cat was limping on his right front leg because the whole paw and its claws were missing; so he asked:
“What have you done with your paw?”
The Cat wanted to answer something, but got muddled. Then the Fox said at once:

“My friend is too modest, and that is why he doesn’t answer. I’ll answer for him. You see, an hour ago we met an old wolf on the road, almost fainting with hunger, who asked us for something to eat. Since we didn’t have even a fishbone to give him, what did my friend, who truly has a heart as generous as Caesar’s, do? He bit off a paw from one of his front legs and threw it to that poor creature, so he could have a meal.”
