And as the Fox said this, he wiped away a tear.
Pinocchio, moved as well, went up to the Cat and whispered in his ear:
“If all cats were like you, how lucky mice would be!”
“And what are you doing here now?” the Fox asked the puppet.
“I’m waiting for my father, who should arrive here at any moment.”
“And your gold coins?”
“They’re still in my pocket, except for one I spent at the Red Crayfish Inn.”
“And to think that instead of four coins, they could be a thousand or two thousand tomorrow! Why don’t you take my advice? Why don’t you go and plant them in the Field of Miracles?”
“I can’t today: I’ll go another day.”
“Another day will be too late!” said the Fox.
“Why?”
“Because that field has been bought by a rich gentleman, and from tomorrow onwards no one will be allowed to plant money there any more.”
“How far is the Field of Miracles from here?”

“Only two kilometres. Will you come with us? You’ll be there in half an hour: you plant the four coins straight away: after a few minutes you collect two thousand, and this evening you come back here with your pockets full. Will you come with us?”

Pinocchio hesitated a little before answering, because he remembered the good Fairy, old Geppetto and the Talking Cricket’s warnings; but in the end he did what all children with no sense and no heart do; that is, he gave his head a little shake and said to the Fox and the Cat:
“Let’s go; I’ll come with you.”
And they set off.

After walking for half a day, they reached a town called “Foolcatcher.” As soon as he entered the town, Pinocchio saw all the streets filled with dogs with patchy fur yawning with hunger, sheep with their wool cut off trembling with cold, hens without combs or wattles begging for a grain of corn, large butterflies that could no longer fly because they had sold their beautiful coloured wings, peacocks with no tails who were ashamed to show themselves, and pheasants creeping quietly along, mourning their shining gold and silver feathers, now lost for ever.
Among this crowd of beggars and ashamed poor creatures, fine carriages passed from time to time, carrying a Fox, a thieving Magpie or some ugly bird of prey.
“And where is the Field of Miracles?” asked Pinocchio.
“Just a few steps from here.”
No sooner said than done, they crossed the town and, going outside its walls, stopped in an empty field that looked more or less like any other field.
“Here we are,” the Fox said to the puppet. “Now bend down, dig a little hole in the field with your hands, and put the gold coins in it.”
Pinocchio obeyed. He dug the hole, put in the four gold coins he had left, and then covered the hole with a little earth.
“Now,” said the Fox, “go to the water channel nearby, fetch a bucket of water and water the ground where you have planted them.”
Pinocchio went to the water channel and, because he had no bucket handy, took a slipper off his foot, filled it with water and watered the earth covering the hole. Then he asked:
“Is there anything else to do?”
“Nothing else,” replied the Fox. “Now we can leave. You come back here in about twenty minutes, and you’ll find the little tree already growing out of the ground, with its branches covered in coins.”
The poor puppet, beside himself with joy, thanked the Fox and the Cat a thousand times and promised them a wonderful present.
“We don’t want presents,” replied the two scoundrels. “It is enough for us to have taught you how to become rich without any hard work, and we couldn’t be happier.”
Having said this, they said goodbye to Pinocchio, wished him a good harvest and went about their business.
chapters.title: Pinocchio meets the Fox and the Cat again and goes with them to plant the four coins in the Field of Miracles.

paragraphs: The puppet returned to town and began counting the minutes one by one: and when he thought it was time, he immediately took the road back to the Field of Miracles.
And as he hurried along, his heart beat hard, going tick, tock, tick, tock, like a grandfather clock when it is really racing. And meanwhile he thought to himself:

“And what if, instead of a thousand coins, I found two thousand on the tree’s branches? And what if, instead of two thousand, I found five thousand? And what if, instead of five thousand, I found a hundred thousand? What a fine gentleman I would become! I’d like a beautiful palace, a thousand little wooden horses and a thousand stables to play with, a cellar full of sweet rose liqueur and red spice liqueur, and a bookcase full of candied fruit, cakes, sweet fruit breads, almond sweets and rolled wafers with cream.”

Dreaming like this, he came near the field and stopped to see whether he could spot a tree with branches loaded with coins: but he saw nothing. He took another hundred steps, and nothing; he entered the field… went right up to the little hole where he had buried his gold coins, and nothing. Then he grew worried and, forgetting the rules of manners and good behaviour, took a hand out of his pocket and gave his head a very long scratch.
Just then he heard a loud laugh ringing in his ears: and looking up, he saw a large parrot in a tree, picking pests out of the few feathers it had left.
“Why are you laughing?” Pinocchio asked crossly.
“I’m laughing because while cleaning my feathers, I tickled myself under my wings.”
The puppet did not answer. He went to the water channel and, filling the same slipper with water, began watering the earth covering the gold coins again.
Then another laugh, even ruder than the first, rang out in the quiet emptiness of the field.
“Now then,” shouted Pinocchio, growing angry, “will you tell me, you rude Parrot, what you’re laughing at?”
“I’m laughing at those fools who believe every bit of nonsense and let themselves be trapped by anyone cleverer than they are.”
“Are you talking about me?”

“Yes, I’m talking about you, poor Pinocchio: you, who are silly enough to believe that money can be planted and harvested in fields, just like beans and pumpkins. I believed it once too, and today I’m paying for it. Today, though too late, I’ve had to accept that to put together a little money honestly, you must know how to earn it, either by working with your own hands or by using your own head.”
“I don’t understand you,” said the puppet, who was already beginning to tremble with fear.

“Oh well! I’ll explain more clearly,” added the Parrot. “You see, while you were in town, the Fox and the Cat came back to this field: they took the buried gold coins, and then ran away like the wind. And now, good luck to anyone trying to catch them!”

Pinocchio’s mouth fell open, and, refusing to believe the Parrot’s words, he began digging with his hands and nails in the ground he had watered. And digging, digging, digging, he made a hole so deep that a haystack could have fitted into it upright: but the coins were gone.
Then, filled with despair, he ran back to town and went straight to the courthouse to report the two scoundrels who had robbed him to the judge.

The judge was a large ape of the gorilla family: an old ape respected for his great age, his white beard and especially his golden glasses, without lenses, which he had to wear all the time because of sore, watering eyes that had troubled him for several years.

Standing before the judge, Pinocchio told every detail of the wicked trick that had been played on him; he gave the names, surnames and descriptions of the scoundrels, and ended by asking for justice.
The judge listened very kindly; he took a great interest in the story: his heart softened, and he was moved: and when the puppet had nothing more to say, he reached out his hand and rang a bell.
At the sound of the bell, two mastiff dogs dressed as policemen appeared at once.
Then the judge pointed Pinocchio out to the policemen and said:
“That poor fellow has been robbed of four gold coins: so take him and put him in prison at once.”
The puppet, hearing this sentence fall on him out of nowhere, was stunned and wanted to protest: but the policemen, to avoid wasting time, covered his mouth and took him to jail.

And there he had to stay for four months: four very long months: and he would have stayed even longer, if something very lucky had not happened. For you should know that the young Emperor who ruled the town of Foolcatcher, having won a great victory over his enemies, ordered big public celebrations, lights, fireworks, horse races and bicycle races, and, as an extra sign of joy, ordered the prisons opened and all the criminals let out.
“If the others are getting out of prison, I want to get out too,” Pinocchio said to the jailer.
“Not you,” replied the jailer, “because you’re not one of that fine crowd…”
“I beg your pardon,” replied Pinocchio, “I’m a criminal too.”
“In that case you’re quite right,” said the jailer; and taking off his cap respectfully and bowing to him, he opened the prison doors and let him go.
chapters.title: Pinocchio is robbed of his gold coins, and as punishment gets four months in prison.

paragraphs: Imagine Pinocchio’s joy when he found himself free. Without stopping to discuss this or that, he left the town at once and took the road that would lead him back to the Fairy’s little house.
Because of the drizzly weather, the road had become a sea of mud that came halfway up his legs.
But the puppet paid no attention to it.
Desperate to see his father and his blue-haired little sister again, he ran in leaps like a greyhound, and as he ran, the mud splashed right up to his cap. Meanwhile he kept saying to himself:

“So many terrible things have happened to me… And I deserve them! Because I’m a stubborn, headstrong puppet… I always want to do everything my own way, without listening to the people who love me and have a thousand times more sense than I do! But from now on, I’m determined to change my life and become a well-behaved, obedient boy! After all, I’ve already seen that children who disobey always come off worse and never get anything right. And will my father have waited for me? Will I find him at the Fairy’s house? It’s so long since I last saw the poor man, and I’m longing to give him a thousand hugs and smother him with kisses! And will the Fairy forgive the bad thing I did to her? To think that she has given me so much attention and loving care… and to think that if I’m still alive today, I owe it to her! Could there be a more ungrateful, heartless boy than me?”
As he was saying this, he suddenly stopped in fright and took four steps backwards.
What had he seen?
He had seen a huge snake lying across the road, with green skin, fiery eyes and a pointed tail that smoked like a chimney.

It is impossible to imagine the puppet’s fear: he went more than half a kilometre away and sat on a little pile of stones, waiting for the snake to finally go about its business and leave the road clear.
He waited one hour; two hours; three hours: but the snake was still there, and even from far away he could see the red glow of its fiery eyes and the column of smoke rising from the tip of its tail.
Then Pinocchio, imagining himself brave, came within a few steps and, in a soft, gentle, coaxing little voice, said to the snake:
“Excuse me, Mr Snake, would you please move a little to one side, just enough to let me pass?”
He might as well have spoken to a wall. No one moved.
Then he tried again in the same little voice:
“You should know, Mr Snake, that I’m going home, where my father is waiting for me, and I haven’t seen him for a very long time! So would you mind letting me go on my way?”

He waited for some sign of an answer to that question: but no answer came: instead, the snake, which until then had seemed lively and full of life, grew still and almost stiff. Its eyes closed, and its tail stopped smoking.

“Can it really be dead?” said Pinocchio, rubbing his hands with joy; and without wasting any time, he began to step over it to get to the other side of the road. But before he had finished lifting his leg, the snake suddenly reared up like a released spring: and the puppet, jumping back in fright, tripped and fell to the ground.
And he fell so awkwardly that his head was stuck in the road’s mud, with his legs straight up in the air.

At the sight of that upside-down puppet kicking his legs at an unbelievable speed, the snake burst into such wild laughter that he laughed and laughed and laughed until, from the effort of laughing too much, a vein in his chest burst: and this time he really died.

Then Pinocchio began running again to reach the Fairy’s house before dark. But along the road, unable to bear the terrible pains of hunger any longer, he jumped into a field, intending to pick a few bunches of muscat grapes. If only he had never done it!
As soon as he reached the vine, snap!… he felt two sharp iron jaws close around his legs, making him see every star in the sky.
The poor puppet had been caught in a trap that some farmers had set there to catch the large stone martens that were a menace to every chicken in the neighbourhood.
chapters.title: Freed from prison, he sets off for the Fairy’s house; but along the way he meets a horrible snake, and then gets caught in a trap.

paragraphs: Pinocchio, as you can imagine, began to cry, scream and beg for help: but his tears and cries were useless, because there were no houses in sight and not a living soul passed along the road.
Meanwhile, night fell.

Partly from the pain of the trap cutting into his shins, and partly from the fear of being alone in the dark among those fields, the puppet was almost beginning to faint: when suddenly, seeing a firefly pass above his head, he called to it and said:
“Oh, little firefly, would you be kind enough to free me from this suffering?”
“Poor child!” replied the firefly, stopping to look at him with pity. “How did you get your legs caught between those sharp iron jaws?”
“I came into the field to pick two bunches of these muscat grapes, and…”
“But were the grapes yours?”
“No…”
“Then who taught you to take other people’s things?”
“I was hungry…”
“Hunger, my boy, is not a good reason to take things that do not belong to us…”
“That’s true, that’s true!” cried Pinocchio, weeping. “But I won’t do it again.”

At this point, the conversation was interrupted by the very faint sound of approaching footsteps. It was the owner of the field, coming on tiptoe to see whether one of those stone martens that ate his chickens at night had been caught in the trap.
And he was very surprised when, taking his lantern out from under his overcoat, he saw that instead of a stone marten, a boy had been caught.
“Ah, you little thief!” said the farmer angrily. “So you’re the one who steals my hens?”
“Not me, not me!” cried Pinocchio, sobbing. “I only came into the field to take two bunches of grapes!”
“Anyone who steals grapes is quite capable of stealing chickens too. Leave it to me, I’ll teach you a lesson you’ll remember for a long time.”
And opening the trap, he grabbed the puppet by the back of the neck and carried him all the way home, just as you would carry a baby lamb.
When he reached the yard in front of the house, he flung him to the ground: and keeping a foot on his neck, he said:

“It’s late now and I want to go to bed. We’ll settle our business tomorrow. Meanwhile, since the dog that guarded my house at night died today, you will take his place straight away. You will be my watchdog.”

No sooner said than done, he put a thick collar covered in brass spikes around his neck and tightened it so he could not pull his head through it to take it off. A long iron chain was attached to the collar: and the chain was fixed to the wall.

“If it starts to rain tonight,” said the farmer, “you can go and lie down in that wooden kennel, where there is still the straw that my poor dog slept on for four years. And if thieves should happen to come, remember to keep your ears open and bark.”

After this last warning, the farmer went into the house and bolted the door firmly: and poor Pinocchio stayed crouching in the yard, more dead than alive from cold, hunger and fear. And from time to time, angrily thrusting his hands inside the collar that squeezed his throat, he said through his tears:

“It serves me right! Sadly, it serves me right! I chose to be lazy and wander about… I chose to listen to bad companions, and that is why bad luck always follows me. If I had been a good little boy, like so many others; if I had wanted to study and work, if I had stayed at home with my poor father, I wouldn’t be here now, out in the fields, acting as watchdog for a farmer’s house. Oh, if only I could be born all over again! But now it’s too late, and I must put up with it!”
After this little outburst, which came straight from his heart, he went inside the kennel and fell asleep.
chapters.title: Pinocchio is caught by a farmer, who forces him to act as watchdog for a henhouse.

paragraphs: He had already been sleeping soundly for more than two hours when, around midnight, he was woken by whispering and the hush-hush of strange little voices that seemed to come from the yard. Poking the tip of his nose out of the kennel’s opening, he saw four little dark-furred animals, rather like cats, gathered in a meeting. But they were not cats: they were stone martens, little meat-eating animals very fond of eggs and young hens. One of these martens left its companions, came to the kennel’s opening and said quietly:
“Good evening, Melampo.”
“My name isn’t Melampo,” replied the puppet.
“Then who are you?”
“I’m Pinocchio.”
“And what are you doing there?”
“I’m acting as watchdog.”
“And where is Melampo? Where is the old dog who lived in this kennel?”
“He died this morning.”
“Died? Poor creature! He was so good! But judging by your face, you seem to be a decent dog too.”
“Excuse me, I’m not a dog!”
“Then what are you?”
“I’m a puppet.”
“And you’re acting as watchdog?”
“Sadly, yes: as my punishment!”
“Well then, I offer you the same deal I had with the late Melampo, and you’ll be pleased.”
“And what was that deal?”

“We’ll come once a week, as we used to, to visit this henhouse at night, and we’ll take away eight hens. We’ll eat seven of these hens and give one to you, on the condition, of course, that you pretend to be asleep and never get the idea of barking and waking the farmer.”
“And did Melampo really do that?” asked Pinocchio.

“He did, and we always got along with him. So sleep peacefully, and be sure that before we leave, we’ll put a hen on your kennel, already plucked, for your breakfast tomorrow. Do we understand each other?”
“Only too well!” replied Pinocchio: and he shook his head in a rather threatening way, as if he meant to say, “We’ll talk again very soon!”

When the four martens thought everything was safely arranged, they went straight to the henhouse, which stood very close to the dog’s kennel; and forcing open the little wooden door with their teeth and claws, they slipped inside one after another. But they had hardly finished entering when they heard the little door slam shut very hard.
It was Pinocchio who had shut it; and, not satisfied with shutting it, he pushed a large stone in front of it as a prop, to make extra sure.
Then he began to bark: and, barking just like a watchdog, he went woof-woof-woof-woof.
At that barking, the farmer jumped out of bed, took his gun and came to the window, asking:
“What’s happening?”
“There are thieves!” replied Pinocchio.
“Where are they?”
“In the henhouse.”
“I’m coming down at once.”
And indeed, before you could say amen, the farmer came down: he rushed into the henhouse and, after catching the four martens and shutting them in a sack, said to them with real delight:

“At last you’ve fallen into my hands! I could punish you, but I’m not so cruel! Instead, I’ll be content to take you tomorrow to the innkeeper in the nearby village, who will skin you and cook you like hare in sweet-and-sour sauce. It’s an honour you don’t deserve, but generous men like me don’t bother about such little things!”
Then he went up to Pinocchio, began patting him kindly, and among other things asked:
“How did you discover those four little thieves’ plan? And to think that Melampo, my faithful Melampo, never noticed anything!”

The puppet could then have told what he knew; that is, he could have told about the shameful deal between the dog and the martens; but remembering that the dog was dead, he immediately thought to himself, “What’s the use of accusing the dead? The dead are dead, and the best thing we can do is leave them in peace!”
“When the martens arrived in the yard, were you awake or asleep?” the farmer went on asking.

“Asleep,” replied Pinocchio, “but the martens woke me with their chatter, and one came right up to the kennel to tell me, ‘If you promise not to bark and not to wake the master, we’ll give you a young hen, already plucked!’ Do you understand? The cheek of making a suggestion like that to me! Because you should know that I’m a puppet who may have every fault in the world: but I will never have the fault of joining in with dishonest people and helping them steal!”
“Good boy!” cried the farmer, patting him on the shoulder. “Those feelings do you credit: and to show you how pleased I am, I’m setting you free right now to go home.”
And he took off the dog collar.
chapters.title: Pinocchio discovers the thieves and is set free as a reward for being faithful.

figures.alt: Pinocchio flies over the coast on the Pigeon’s back.

paragraphs: As soon as Pinocchio no longer felt the cruel, shameful weight of that collar around his neck, he ran off across the fields, and did not stop for a single minute until he reached the main road that would take him back to the Fairy’s little house.

When he reached the main road, he turned to look down over the plain below, and could clearly see with his own eyes the wood where he had so unfortunately met the Fox and the Cat: he saw the top of the Great Oak rising among the trees, the oak from which he had hung swinging by his neck; but though he looked this way and that, he could not see the little house of the lovely Girl with the blue hair.

Then he had a sad feeling that something was wrong; and running with all the strength left in his legs, he reached in a few minutes the meadow where the little white house had once stood. But the little white house was gone. In its place was a small marble stone, on which these sad words were written in printed letters:
HERE LIES THE GIRL WITH THE BLUE HAIR WHO DIED OF SORROW AFTER BEING ABANDONED BY HER LITTLE BROTHER PINOCCHIO.

How the puppet felt when he had struggled to read those words, I will leave you to imagine. He fell face down on the ground, and covering that gravestone with a thousand kisses, burst into bitter tears. He cried all night, and next morning, as day broke, he was still crying, though his eyes had no tears left: and his cries and sobs were so sharp and heartbreaking that all the hills around echoed them.
And as he cried he said:

“Oh, my dear Fairy, why did you die…? Why didn’t I die instead of you, when I am so bad and you were so good…? And where can my father be? Oh, my dear Fairy, tell me where I can find him, because I want to stay with him always, and never leave him again! Never! Never!… Oh, my dear Fairy, tell me it isn’t true that you’re dead!… If you really love me… if you love your little brother, come back to life… be alive again as you were before! Doesn’t it make you sad to see me alone, abandoned by everyone…? If the murderers come, they’ll hang me from the branch again… and then I’ll die for ever. What do you expect me to do here all alone in this world? Now that I’ve lost you and my father, who will give me food? Where will I sleep at night? Who will make me a new little jacket? Oh! It would be better, a hundred times better, if I died too! Yes, I want to die! Boo-hoo-hoo!”
And as he cried in despair like this, he made as if to tear out his hair: but since his hair was made of wood, he could not even have the satisfaction of digging his fingers into it.
Meanwhile a large Pigeon flew overhead, and stopping with his wings spread, called down to him from a great height:
“Tell me, child, what are you doing down there?”
“Can’t you see? I’m crying!” said Pinocchio, raising his head towards the voice and rubbing his eyes with his jacket sleeve.
“Tell me,” the Pigeon then added, “do you happen to know, among your friends, a puppet called Pinocchio?”
“Pinocchio? Did you say Pinocchio?” repeated the puppet, jumping straight to his feet. “I’m Pinocchio!”
At this answer the Pigeon flew swiftly down and landed on the ground. He was bigger than a turkey.
“Then you must know Geppetto too?” he asked the puppet.
“Do I know him! He’s my poor father! Has he spoken to you about me? Will you take me to him? But is he still alive? Answer me, please; is he still alive?”
“I left him three days ago on the seashore.”
“What was he doing?”

“He was making himself a little boat to cross the ocean. That poor man has been wandering around the world looking for you for more than four months: and as he has never been able to find you, he has now decided to search for you in the far-off countries of the New World.”
“How far is it from here to the shore?” asked Pinocchio, full of love and worry.
“More than a thousand kilometres.”
“A thousand kilometres? Oh, dear Pigeon, how wonderful it would be if I could have your wings!…”
“If you want to come, I’ll take you.”
“How?”
“Riding on my back. Are you very heavy?”
“Heavy? Not at all! I’m as light as a leaf.”

And without another word, Pinocchio jumped onto the Pigeon’s back; and putting one leg on each side, as riders do, he cried happily: “Gallop, gallop, little horse, because I need to get there quickly!…” The Pigeon took off and in a few minutes flew so high that he almost touched the clouds. At that amazing height, the puppet felt curious and turned to look down: and he was so frightened and dizzy that, to keep himself from falling, he wrapped his arms very, very tightly around the neck of his feathered ride.
￼ch23
They flew all day. As evening came, the Pigeon said:
“I’m terribly thirsty!”
“And I’m terribly hungry!” added Pinocchio.
“Let’s stop at this pigeon house for a few minutes; then we’ll set off again, so we can be on the seashore at dawn tomorrow.”
They went into an empty pigeon house, where there was only a basin full of water and a little basket filled with vetch seeds.

In all his life the puppet had never been able to stand vetch seeds: according to him, they made him feel sick and turned his stomach: but that evening he stuffed himself with them, and when he had almost finished them, he turned to the Pigeon and said:
“I’d never have believed vetch seeds could taste so good!”
“You must understand, my boy,” replied the Pigeon, “that when you’re truly hungry and there’s nothing else to eat, even vetch seeds taste delicious! Hunger has no fussy demands or fancy tastes!”
After their quick little meal, they set off again, and away they went! Next morning they reached the seashore.
The Pigeon set Pinocchio down on the ground, and not even wanting the bother of being thanked for a kind deed, immediately flew off again and disappeared.
The beach was full of people shouting and waving their arms as they looked out to sea.
“What’s happened?” Pinocchio asked a little old woman.

“What’s happened is that a poor father, having lost his son, insisted on getting into a little boat to look for him across the sea; and the sea is very rough today, and the little boat is about to sink…”
“Where is the little boat?”
“There it is, straight ahead of my finger,” said the old woman, pointing to a little boat which, at that distance, looked like a nutshell with a tiny, tiny man inside.
Pinocchio fixed his eyes on that spot, and after looking carefully, let out a piercing cry, shouting:
“It’s my father! It’s my father!”

Meanwhile the little boat, battered by the raging waves, vanished among the great breakers, then came floating up again: and Pinocchio, standing on the tip of a high rock, kept calling his father’s name and making signal after signal with his hands and his handkerchief and even the cap on his head.

And it seemed that Geppetto, though he was very far from the beach, recognised his son, because he too took off his cap and waved, and with many gestures made him understand that he would gladly come back, but the sea was so rough that he could not work his oar or get closer to land.
All at once a terrible wave came, and the boat disappeared. They waited for the boat to come up again: but the boat was never seen again.
“Poor man,” said the fishermen gathered on the beach; and murmuring a prayer under their breath, they turned to go home.
Just then they heard a desperate cry, and turning round, saw a little boy throwing himself into the sea from the top of a rock, shouting:
“I want to save my father!”

Being made entirely of wood, Pinocchio floated easily and swam like a fish. One moment they saw him disappear underwater, swept away by the force of the waves, and the next he came up again with a leg or an arm showing, a very long way from land. At last they lost sight of him, and could see him no more.
“Poor boy!” said the fishermen gathered on the beach; and murmuring a prayer under their breath, they went home.
chapters.title: Pinocchio mourns the death of the lovely Girl with the blue hair: then he meets a Pigeon who carries him to the seashore, where he jumps into the water to help his father Geppetto.

paragraphs: Pinocchio, driven by the hope of arriving in time to help his poor father, swam the whole night long.
And what a dreadful night it was! Rain poured down, hail fell, thunder crashed horribly, and the lightning was so bright that it seemed like day.
As morning came, he managed to make out a long strip of land not far away. It was an island in the middle of the sea.

Then he did everything he could to reach that shore: but it was no use. The waves, chasing and climbing over one another, tossed him between them as if he were a twig or a straw. At last, luckily for him, a wave came with such power and force that it hurled him right onto the sand of the shore.
The blow was so hard that, as he hit the ground, all his ribs and joints cracked; but he cheered himself up at once by saying: “I’ve had another lucky escape!”
Meanwhile, little by little, the sky cleared; the sun came out in all its brightness, and the sea grew perfectly calm and smooth as oil.

Then the puppet spread his clothes in the sun to dry them, and began looking this way and that to see whether he could spot a little boat with a little man inside on that enormous stretch of water. But after looking very carefully, he saw nothing before him except sky, sea, and a few ships’ sails, so very, very far away that they looked like flies.

“If only I knew what this island is called!” he kept saying. “If only I knew whether the people on this island are decent, I mean people who don’t have the habit of hanging boys from tree branches! But who can I ask? Who, when there’s nobody here?…”

The thought of being alone, alone, alone in that great empty place made him so sad that he was just about to cry; when all at once he saw a large fish passing a little way from the shore, going calmly about its business with its whole head out of the water.
Not knowing its name, the puppet shouted loudly to make himself heard:
“Hey, Mr Fish, could I have a word?”
“Even two,” answered the fish, who was a Dolphin as polite as any you could find in all the seas of the world.
“Would you please tell me whether there are any towns on this island where you can eat without being in danger of being eaten?”
“There certainly are!” answered the Dolphin. “In fact, you’ll find one not far from here.”
“And which road do I take to get there?”
“You must take that little path there on the left, and keep walking straight ahead. You can’t go wrong.”
“Tell me one more thing. Since you go about the sea all day and all night, have you happened to meet a tiny little boat with my father in it?”
“And who is your father?”
“He’s the best father in the world, just as I’m the worst son there could be.”
“With the storm we had last night,” answered the Dolphin, “the little boat must have sunk.”
“And my father?”
“By now he will have been swallowed by the terrible Shark, who came a few days ago to spread death and misery through our waters.”
“Is this Shark very big?” asked Pinocchio, already beginning to shake with fear.

“Is he big!” replied the Dolphin. “To give you some idea, I’ll tell you that he’s bigger than a five-storey building, and his great mouth is so wide and deep that a whole railway train could easily go through it with its engine running.”
“Oh, goodness!” cried the frightened puppet; and getting dressed in a great hurry, he turned to the Dolphin and said:
“Goodbye, Mr Fish: I’m very sorry to have troubled you, and a thousand thanks for your kindness.”

With that he immediately took the little path and began to walk quickly: so quickly that he seemed almost to be running. And at every tiny sound he heard, he turned straight round to look behind him, afraid of finding himself chased by that terrible Shark as big as a five-storey house and with a railway train in his mouth.

After walking for more than half an hour, he reached a little town called “the town of the Busy Bees”. The streets swarmed with people hurrying this way and that about their business: everyone was working, everyone had something to do. You couldn’t have found a lazy person or someone just hanging about even if you had searched with a little lamp.
“I see,” that lazy Pinocchio said at once, “this town isn’t for me! I wasn’t born to work!”
Meanwhile hunger was tormenting him, because it was now twenty-four hours since he had eaten anything at all; not even a dish of vetch seeds.
What could he do?
There were only two ways left for him to get something to eat: either ask for some work, or beg for a soldo or a mouthful of bread.

He was ashamed to beg: because his father had always taught him that only old people and sick people had the right to ask for charity. The truly poor in this world, who deserve help and pity, are only those who, because of age or illness, can no longer earn their bread by working with their own hands. Everyone else has a duty to work; and if they don’t work and go hungry, so much the worse for them.
Just then a man came along the road, sweating and out of breath, dragging two carts loaded with coal all by himself with great effort.
Pinocchio, judging from his face that he was a kind man, went up to him and, lowering his eyes in shame, said quietly:
“Would you be kind enough to give me a soldo, because I feel as if I’m dying of hunger?”
“Not just one soldo,” answered the coal seller, “but I’ll give you four, if you help me pull these two carts of coal home.”
“Well, really!” answered the puppet, almost offended; “for your information, I’ve never been a donkey; I’ve never pulled a cart!”
“Good for you!” replied the coal seller. “Then, my boy, if you really feel as if you’re dying of hunger, eat two nice slices of your pride, and be careful not to upset your stomach.”
A few minutes later a bricklayer came along the road, carrying a basket of mortar on his shoulders.
“Kind sir, would you give a soldo to a poor boy who is yawning with hunger?”
“Gladly; come and carry mortar with me,” answered the bricklayer, “and instead of one soldo, I’ll give you five.”
“But mortar is heavy,” replied Pinocchio, “and I don’t want to do hard work.”
“If you don’t want to do hard work, then, my boy, enjoy your yawning, and may it do you good.”
In less than half an hour another twenty people passed, and Pinocchio begged a little charity from every one of them, but they all answered:
“Aren’t you ashamed? Instead of hanging about in the street, go and find some work, and learn to earn your bread!”
At last a kind little woman came by, carrying two jugs of water.
“Would you mind, good woman, if I had a sip of water from your jug?” asked Pinocchio, who was burning with thirst.
“Drink, my boy!” said the little woman, putting the two jugs on the ground.
When Pinocchio had soaked up the water like a sponge, he muttered under his breath, wiping his mouth:
“I’ve got rid of my thirst! If only I could get rid of my hunger too!…”
Hearing these words, the kind little woman immediately added:
“If you help me carry one of these jugs of water home, I’ll give you a nice piece of bread.”
Pinocchio looked at the jug and said neither yes nor no.
“And with the bread I’ll give you a nice plate of cauliflower with oil and vinegar,” added the good woman.
Pinocchio glanced at the jug again and said neither yes nor no.
“And after the cauliflower I’ll give you a lovely sweet filled with rose liqueur.”
Pinocchio could no longer resist the promise of this last treat, and making up his mind, he said:
“Oh, all right! I’ll carry the jug home for you!”
The jug was very heavy, and as the puppet was not strong enough to carry it in his hands, he had to settle for carrying it on his head.
When they reached the house, the kind little woman sat Pinocchio at a small table that was already laid, and put the bread, the dressed cauliflower, and the sweet in front of him.
Pinocchio didn’t eat; he swallowed a flood of food. His stomach seemed like a flat that had stood empty and unlived-in for five months.

As the fierce pangs of hunger slowly died down, he raised his head to thank the woman who had helped him: but before he had finished looking into her face, he let out a very long “ohhh!” of amazement, and sat there spellbound, his eyes wide open, his fork in the air, and his mouth full of bread and cauliflower.
“What is all this surprise about?” the good woman said, laughing.

“It’s…” Pinocchio answered, stammering, “it’s… it’s… that you look like… you remind me of… yes, yes, yes, the same voice… the same eyes… the same hair… yes, yes, yes… you too have blue hair… like hers! Oh, my dear Fairy!… Oh, my dear Fairy!… Tell me it’s you, really you!… Don’t make me cry any more! If you only knew! I’ve cried so much, I’ve suffered so much!…”
And as he said this, Pinocchio was crying floods of tears, and dropping to his knees on the floor, he hugged the knees of that mysterious little woman.
chapters.title: Pinocchio reaches the island of the Busy Bees and finds the Fairy again.

paragraphs: At first the good little woman began by saying that she was not the little Fairy with the blue hair: but then, seeing she had been found out and not wanting to keep up the pretence any longer, she finally admitted who she was, and said to Pinocchio:
“You little rascal of a puppet! How ever did you realise it was me?”
“It was how much I love you that told me.”
“You remember, don’t you? You left me as a little girl, and now you find me a woman; so grown-up that I could almost be your mother.”

“And I’m very glad, because then, instead of little sister, I’ll call you my mother. I’ve been longing for so long to have a mother like all the other boys!… But how did you manage to grow up so quickly?”
“It’s a secret.”
“Teach me: I’d like to grow a little too. Can’t you see? I’m still no taller than a soldo’s worth of cheese.”
“But you can’t grow,” replied the Fairy.
“Why?”
“Because puppets never grow. They are born puppets, live as puppets, and die as puppets.”
“Oh! I’m tired of always being a puppet!” cried Pinocchio, giving himself a slap on the head. “It’s time I became a man too…”
“And you will, if you earn it…”
“Really? And what can I do to earn it?”
“Something very easy: get into the habit of being a good little boy.”
“Aren’t I one already?”
“Far from it! Good boys obey, and you, instead…”
“And I never obey.”
“Good boys learn to love studying and working, and you…”
“And I, instead, hang about and wander around all year.”
“Good boys always tell the truth…”
“And I always tell lies.”
“Good boys go to school gladly…”
“And school gives me a stomach ache. But from today I mean to change my life.”
“Do you promise me?”
“I promise. I want to become a good little boy, and I want to make my father happy… Where can my poor father be now?”
“I don’t know.”
“Will I ever be lucky enough to see him again and hug him?”
“I think so: in fact, I’m sure of it.”

At this answer Pinocchio was so very happy that he took the Fairy’s hands and began kissing them so eagerly that he seemed almost beside himself. Then, raising his face and looking at her lovingly, he asked:
“Tell me, Mummy: so it isn’t true that you’re dead?”
“It seems not,” answered the Fairy, smiling.
“If you knew how much it hurt, and how tight my throat felt, when I read ‘here lies’…”

“I know: and that’s why I forgave you. Your true sorrow showed me that you had a good heart: and with children who have good hearts, even if they are a little naughty and have bad habits, there is always something to hope for: that is, you can always hope that they will return to the right path. That is why I came all this way to find you. I will be your mother…”
“Oh, how wonderful!” cried Pinocchio, jumping for joy.
“You will obey me and always do what I tell you.”
“Gladly, gladly, gladly!”
“Starting tomorrow,” added the Fairy, “you will begin by going to school.”
Pinocchio immediately looked a little less happy.
“Then you will choose a craft or a trade that you like…”
Pinocchio grew serious.
“What are you muttering under your breath?” asked the Fairy, sounding annoyed.
“I was saying…” the puppet mumbled quietly, “that it seems a little late for me to go to school now…”
“No, it isn’t. Remember that it is never too late to study and learn.”
“But I don’t want to learn a craft or a trade…”
“Why?”
“Because work seems like hard work to me.”

“My boy,” said the Fairy, “people who say that almost always end up either in prison or in hospital. You should know that everyone in this world, whether born rich or poor, has a duty to do something, to keep busy, to work. Beware of letting laziness take hold of you! Laziness is a terrible illness, and it must be cured at once, while we are still children; otherwise, when we are grown-up, it can no longer be cured.”
These words touched Pinocchio’s heart, and lifting his head eagerly, he said to the Fairy:
“I’ll study, I’ll work, I’ll do everything you tell me, because, after all, I’m tired of a puppet’s life, and I want to become a boy whatever it takes. You’ve promised me, haven’t you?”
“I’ve promised you, and now it’s up to you.”
chapters.title: Pinocchio promises the Fairy to be good and to study, because he is tired of being a puppet and wants to become a good boy.

paragraphs: The next day Pinocchio went to the town school.

Imagine those little rascals when they saw a puppet come into their school! They laughed and laughed without stopping. One played one trick on him, another played another: one snatched his cap from his hand; another tugged at the back of his jacket; one tried to paint two great moustaches under his nose with ink, and another even dared to tie strings to his hands and feet to make him dance.
For a while Pinocchio acted as if he didn’t mind and let it pass; but at last, feeling his patience slip away, he turned to the boys who were pestering and mocking him most, and said firmly:
“Listen, boys: I didn’t come here to be your clown. I respect other people, and I want to be respected.”
“Well done, Berlicche! You speak like a printed book!” shouted the rascals, helpless with wild laughter: and one of them, ruder than the rest, reached out to grab the puppet by the tip of his nose.
But he was not quick enough: because Pinocchio stretched his leg out under the table and gave him a kick in the shins.
“Ow! What hard feet!” yelled the boy, rubbing the bruise the puppet had given him.
“And what elbows!… Even harder than his feet!” said another, who had got an elbow in the stomach for his nasty tricks.

The fact is that after that kick and that jab of the elbow, Pinocchio immediately won the respect and friendship of all the boys at school: and they all made a great fuss of him, and they all loved him dearly.
And the teacher praised him too, because he found him attentive, hardworking, and clever, always the first to enter the school, always the last to stand up when lessons were over.
His only fault was that he spent time with too many schoolmates; and among them were many troublemakers well known for having little wish to study or do well.
The teacher warned him every day, and the good Fairy too never failed to tell him, over and over again:
“Be careful, Pinocchio! Those bad schoolfriends of yours will sooner or later make you lose your love of studying, and perhaps even land you in serious trouble.”
“No danger of that!” the puppet would answer with a shrug, tapping the middle of his forehead with his finger, as if to say: “There’s plenty of sense in here!”
Now it happened that one fine day, as he was walking to school, he met a group of his usual schoolmates, who came up to him and said:
“Have you heard the big news?”
“No.”
“A Shark as big as a mountain has come to the sea near here.”
“Really?… Could it be the same Shark from when my poor father drowned?”
“We’re going to the shore to see it. Do you want to come too?”
“Not me: I want to go to school.”
“What do you care about school? We’ll go to school tomorrow. One lesson more or one lesson less, we’ll still be the same donkeys.”
“And what will the teacher say?”
“Let the teacher talk. He’s paid to grumble every day.”
“And my mother?”
“Mothers never know anything,” answered those troublemakers.
“Do you know what I’ll do?” said Pinocchio. “I want to see the Shark for reasons of my own… but I’ll go and see it after school.”

“You poor fool!” one of the group shot back. “Do you think a fish that size will wait around to suit you? As soon as he gets bored, he heads straight off somewhere else, and then it’s goodbye to him.”
“How long does it take to get from here to the shore?” asked the puppet.
“In an hour we’ll be there and back.”
“Then let’s go! And whoever runs fastest is the best!” cried Pinocchio.

With that signal to start, the group of rascals, carrying their books and exercise books under their arms, began running across the fields, and Pinocchio was always ahead of them all, as if he had wings on his feet.

Now and then he turned round and teased his friends, who were a long way behind, and seeing them panting, breathless, dusty, and with their tongues hanging out, he laughed with all his heart. The poor fool had no idea at that moment what terrors and terrible troubles he was heading towards.
chapters.title: Pinocchio goes to the seashore with his schoolmates to see the terrible Shark.

paragraphs: As soon as he reached the beach, Pinocchio took a long look out to sea; but he saw no Shark. The sea was as smooth as a great sheet of mirror glass.
“Well, where is the Shark?” he asked, turning to his schoolmates.
“He must have gone to have breakfast,” one of them answered, laughing.
“Or he’s thrown himself onto his bed for a little nap,” added another, laughing louder than ever.
From those silly answers and that stupid laughter, Pinocchio understood that his schoolmates had played a nasty trick on him by making him believe something untrue; and feeling hurt, he said angrily:
“Well, then? What did you get out of making me believe that story about the Shark?”
“We certainly got something out of it!” the rascals answered together.
“And what was that?”
“Making you miss school and come with us. Aren’t you ashamed to turn up so regularly and work so hard in class every day? Aren’t you ashamed to study as much as you do?”
“And if I study, what does it matter to you?”
“It matters a great deal to us, because you make us look bad in front of the teacher…”
“Why?”
“Because pupils who study always show up those like us who don’t want to study. And we don’t want to be shown up! We have our pride too!”
“So what must I do to please you?”
“You must get tired of school, lessons, and the teacher too, because those are our three great enemies.”
“And if I want to go on studying?”
“We won’t even look at you again, and at the first chance we’ll make you pay.”
“Really, you almost make me laugh,” said the puppet with a little shake of his head.

“Hey, Pinocchio!” shouted the biggest of the boys, coming right up to his face. “Don’t come here showing off: don’t come here acting like such a little fighting cock!… Because if you aren’t afraid of us, we aren’t afraid of you either! Remember, there’s only one of you and seven of us.”
“Seven, like the deadly sins,” said Pinocchio with a loud laugh.
“Did you hear? He’s insulted us all! He’s called us deadly sins!”
“Pinocchio! Apologise for insulting us… or you’ll be sorry!”
“Cuckoo!” said the puppet, tapping the tip of his nose with his finger to mock them.
“Pinocchio! This will end badly!”
“Cuckoo!”
“You’ll get a beating fit for a donkey!”
“Cuckoo!”
“You’ll go home with a broken nose!”
“Cuckoo!”
“I’ll give you cuckoo!” shouted the boldest of the rascals. “Take this to start with, and save it for your supper tonight.”
And as he said it, he punched him in the head.
But it was, as the saying goes, a blow for a blow; because the puppet, as you would expect, immediately answered with another punch: and all at once everyone was fighting fiercely.

Although he was alone, Pinocchio defended himself like a hero. He used his very hard wooden feet so well that he always kept his enemies at a respectful distance. Wherever his feet could reach and land, they always left a bruise as a souvenir.

Then the boys, annoyed that they could not fight the puppet at close range, thought it best to start throwing things; and untying their bundles of schoolbooks, they began hurling their spelling books, grammar books, Giannettino books, Minuzzolo books, Thouar’s Stories, Baccini’s Little Chick, and other schoolbooks at him: but the puppet, who had quick eyes and knew a trick or two, always ducked in time, so that the books flew over his head and all landed in the sea.

Imagine the fish! Thinking those books were something to eat, the fish rushed in crowds to the surface; but after biting into a few pages or a title page, they immediately spat them out again, pulling a face that seemed to say: “This isn’t food for us: we’re used to eating much better than this!”
Meanwhile the fight grew fiercer and fiercer, when a large Crab, who had come out of the water and slowly climbed onto the beach, shouted in a voice like a trombone with a cold:
“Stop it, you little rascals! These fights between boys hardly ever end well. Something bad always happens!”
Poor Crab! He might as well have been talking to the wind. In fact, that rascal Pinocchio turned round to glare at him and said rudely:
“Be quiet, you boring Crab! You’d do better to suck a couple of lichen throat sweets to cure that cold in your throat. Go to bed instead, and try to sweat it out!”
Meanwhile the boys, who had now thrown all their own books, spotted the puppet’s bundle of books a little way off, and grabbed it in less time than it takes to tell.
Among those books was one bound in thick cardboard, with a parchment spine and corners. It was an Arithmetic Textbook. I’ll leave you to imagine how heavy it was!

One of the rascals grabbed that book and, aiming at Pinocchio’s head, threw it with all the strength in his arm: but instead of hitting the puppet, it struck one of his schoolmates on the head, and the boy turned as white as a freshly washed cloth and said only these words:
“Oh, Mummy… help me, because I’m dying!…” Then he fell flat on the sand of the shore.
At the sight of that little lifeless body, the frightened boys took to their heels, and within a few minutes they were out of sight.

But Pinocchio stayed there; and though he too was more dead than alive with grief and fear, he ran to soak his handkerchief in the seawater and began bathing his poor schoolmate’s temple. And meanwhile, crying bitterly and in despair, he called him by name and said:

“Eugenio!… My poor Eugenio!… Open your eyes and look at me!… Why don’t you answer? It wasn’t me, you know, who hurt you so badly! Believe me, it wasn’t me!… Open your eyes, Eugenio… If you keep your eyes shut, you’ll make me die too… Oh, my God! How can I go home now?… How will I dare face my good mother? What will become of me?… Where can I run?… Where can I hide?… Oh, how much better, a thousand times better, it would have been if I’d gone to school!… Why did I listen to these friends, who are the ruin of me? And the teacher told me!… And my mother repeated it: ‘Beware of bad friends!’ But I’m stubborn… a stubborn fool… I let everyone talk, and then I always do as I please! And afterwards I have to pay for it… And so, ever since I came into the world, I haven’t had a quarter of an hour’s peace. My God! What will become of me, what will become of me, what will become of me?”
And Pinocchio went on crying, yelling, hitting himself on the head, and calling poor Eugenio’s name, when suddenly he heard the dull sound of footsteps coming closer.
He turned round: there were two policemen.
“What are you doing lying on the ground like that?” they asked Pinocchio.
“I’m helping my schoolmate.”
“Has he been taken ill?”
“It seems so!…”
“More than ill!” said one of the policemen, bending down and looking closely at Eugenio. “This boy has been wounded in the temple: who hurt him?”
“Not me!” stammered the puppet, who could hardly breathe.
“If it wasn’t you, then who hurt him?”
“Not me!” repeated Pinocchio.
“And what was he hit with?”
“This book.” And the puppet picked the Arithmetic Textbook, bound in cardboard and parchment, up from the ground to show the policeman.
“And whose book is this?”
“Mine.”
“That’s enough: we need nothing more. Get up at once and come with us.”
“But I…”
“Come with us!”
“But I’m innocent…”
“Come with us!”
Before leaving, the policemen called to some fishermen who happened to be passing in their boat close to the shore, and said:
“We’re leaving this boy with the head wound in your care. Take him home and look after him. We’ll come to see him tomorrow.”
Then they turned to Pinocchio and, after placing him between them, ordered him in a military voice:
“Forward! And walk quickly! Or it’ll be worse for you!”

Without needing to be told again, the puppet began walking along the little path that led to the town. But the poor fellow hardly knew what world he was in. He felt as if he were dreaming, and what a terrible dream! He was beside himself. His eyes saw everything double: his legs shook: his tongue stuck to the roof of his mouth, and he could not get out a single word. Yet amid that numbness and confusion, a sharp thorn pierced his heart: the thought, that is, of having to pass beneath the windows of his good Fairy’s house between two policemen. He would rather have died.
They had reached the town and were about to enter it, when a rough gust of wind snatched the cap off Pinocchio’s head and carried it about ten steps away.
“Would you mind,” the puppet said to the policemen, “if I went to get my cap?”
“Go ahead; but be quick about it.”

The puppet went and picked up his cap… but instead of putting it on his head, he put it in his mouth between his teeth, and then began running at full speed towards the seashore. He shot away like a bullet.

The policemen, thinking it would be hard to catch him, set a large mastiff after him, a dog who had won first prize in every dog race. Pinocchio ran, and the dog ran faster than he did; so everyone leaned out of the windows and crowded into the street, eager to see how such a fierce race would end. But they did not get their wish, because the mastiff and Pinocchio raised such a cloud of dust along the road that after a few minutes nothing could be seen at all.
chapters.title: A great fight breaks out between Pinocchio and his schoolmates: one of them is hurt, and Pinocchio is arrested by the police.

paragraphs: During that desperate race there was one terrible moment, a moment when Pinocchio thought he was lost: because you must know that Alidoro (that was the mastiff’s name), by running and running, had almost caught him.
It is enough to say that the puppet could hear the fierce animal panting behind him, only a hand’s width away, and could even feel the hot blasts of his breath.
Luckily the beach was now close, and the sea was only a few steps away.

As soon as he reached the beach, the puppet made a splendid leap, just as a frog might, and landed in the water. Alidoro, instead, wanted to stop: but the force of his run carried him into the water too. And the poor creature could not swim; so he immediately began flailing his paws to stay afloat; but the more he flailed, the more his head went underwater.
When he managed to get his head out again, the poor dog’s eyes were wild with fear, and he barked and cried:
“I’m drowning! I’m drowning!”
“Then die!” Pinocchio answered from far away, now feeling safe from all danger.
“Help me, dear Pinocchio!… Save me from death!…”
At those heartbreaking cries, the puppet, who deep down had a very good heart, felt sorry for him, and turning to the dog, said:
“But if I help save you, do you promise not to bother me or chase me any more?”
“I promise! I promise! Hurry, please, because if you wait another half-minute, I’ll be dead.”

Pinocchio hesitated a little: but then, remembering that his father had told him many times that you never lose by doing a good deed, he swam over to Alidoro, and taking hold of his tail with both hands, brought him safe and sound onto the dry sand of the shore.

The poor dog could no longer stand. Without meaning to, he had swallowed so much salt water that he was swollen like a balloon. But the puppet, not wanting to trust him too much, thought it wise to jump back into the sea; and swimming away from the beach, he called to the friend he had saved:
“Goodbye, Alidoro; have a good journey, and give my greetings to everyone at home.”

“Goodbye, Pinocchio,” answered the dog, “a thousand thanks for saving me from death. You’ve done me a great favour: and in this world, what is done is repaid. If the chance comes, we’ll speak of it again…”

Pinocchio kept swimming, always staying near the land. At last he thought he had reached a safe place: and glancing at the shore, he saw a sort of cave among the rocks, with a long plume of smoke coming out of it.
“There must be a fire in that cave,” he said to himself. “All the better! I’ll go and dry myself and get warm, and then?… And then whatever happens will happen.”

Having made up his mind, he went towards the rocks; but just as he was about to climb up, he felt something underwater rising, rising, rising, and lifting him into the air. He immediately tried to escape, but it was too late now, because to his great surprise he found himself trapped inside a big net among a mass of fish of every shape and size, wagging their tails and struggling like so many desperate souls.

At the same time he saw a fisherman come out of the cave, so ugly, so very ugly, that he looked like a sea monster. Instead of hair, he had a thick bush of green grass on his head; the skin of his body was green, his eyes were green, and his very long beard, reaching all the way down here, was green too. He looked like a large green lizard standing on its hind legs.
When the fisherman had pulled the net out of the sea, he cried happily:
“Blessed Providence! Today too I’ll be able to feast on fish!”
“Good thing I’m not a fish!” Pinocchio said to himself, feeling a little braver.
The net full of fish was carried into the cave, a dark, smoky cave with a great frying pan of oil sizzling in the middle, giving off a smell like burnt candle wicks that took your breath away.
“Now let’s see what fish we’ve caught!” said the green fisherman; and pushing a huge hand into the net, a hand as large as a baker’s shovel, he pulled out a handful of red mullet.
“Lovely red mullet!” he said, looking at them and sniffing them happily. And after sniffing them, he threw them into a tub with no water in it.
Then he repeated the same thing several times; and as he pulled out the other fish, his mouth watered, and he said with delight:
“Lovely hake!…”
“Wonderful grey mullet!…”
“Delicious sole!…”
“Splendid young sea bass!…”
“Pretty little anchovies, heads and all!”
As you can imagine, the hake, grey mullet, sole, young sea bass, and anchovies all went in a heap into the tub to keep the red mullet company.
The last one left in the net was Pinocchio.
As soon as the fisherman pulled him out, he opened his great green eyes wide with surprise and cried, almost frightened:
“What kind of fish is this? I don’t remember ever eating a fish shaped like this.”
And he looked at him carefully again, and after examining him closely from every side, he finally said:
“I see; it must be a sea crab.”
Then Pinocchio, upset at being mistaken for a crab, said crossly:
“What do you mean, a crab? Look how you’re treating me! For your information, I’m a puppet.”
“A puppet?” repeated the fisherman. “To tell the truth, a puppet-fish is a new fish to me! All the better! I’ll enjoy eating you even more.”
“Eat me? But can’t you understand that I’m not a fish? Can’t you hear that I talk and think just as you do?”
“That’s quite true,” added the fisherman, “and since I see you’re a fish, and you’re lucky enough to talk and think like me, I want to show you proper respect too.”
“And what sort of respect would that be?…”
“As a sign of friendship and special respect, I’ll let you choose how you want to be cooked. Would you like to be fried in the pan, or would you rather be cooked in a pot with tomato sauce?”
“To tell the truth,” answered Pinocchio, “if I’m to choose, I’d much rather be set free so I can go home.”

“You’re joking! Do you think I want to lose the chance to taste such a rare fish? A puppet-fish doesn’t turn up in these seas every day. Leave it to me: I’ll fry you in the pan with all the other fish, and you’ll be pleased. Being fried in company is always a comfort.”

At this speech, poor Pinocchio began crying, screaming, and begging: and as he cried he said: “How much better it would have been if I’d gone to school!… I chose to listen to my friends, and now I’m paying for it!… Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!… Boo-hoo!…”

And because he wriggled like an eel and struggled with all his might to slip from the green fisherman’s claws, the fisherman took a good strip of rush fibre and, after tying his hands and feet like a sausage, threw him into the bottom of the tub with the others.
Then, taking out a rough wooden tray full of flour, he began coating all the fish in flour: and as he coated each one, he threw it into the pan to fry.

The first to dance in the boiling oil were the poor hake: then came the young sea bass, then the grey mullet, then the sole and anchovies, and then it was Pinocchio’s turn. Seeing himself so close to death (and such a horrible death!), he shook so much and was so frightened that he had neither voice nor breath left to beg.

The poor boy begged with his eyes! But the green fisherman, without even noticing, rolled him five or six times in the flour, covering him so thoroughly from head to foot that he looked like a puppet made of plaster.
Then he took him by the head, and…
chapters.title: Pinocchio is in danger of being fried in a pan like a fish.

paragraphs: Just as the fisherman was about to throw Pinocchio into the frying pan, a large dog came into the cave, drawn by the strong, tempting smell of frying fish.
“Get out!” the fisherman shouted, threatening him while still holding the flour-covered puppet in his hand.
But the poor dog was hungry enough for four, and as he whined and wagged his tail, he seemed to be saying:
“Give me a bite of fried fish and I’ll leave you alone.”
“Get out, I tell you!” the fisherman repeated; and he stretched out his leg to kick him.
Then the dog, who was not used to putting up with nonsense when he was really hungry, turned on the fisherman with a growl, showing his terrible fangs.
At that moment a very faint little voice was heard in the cave, saying:
“Save me, Alidoro! If you don’t save me, I’m fried!…”
The dog recognised Pinocchio’s voice at once, and realised to his great surprise that it came from the flour-covered bundle the fisherman was holding.
So what does he do? He leaps from the ground, grabs the flour-covered bundle in his mouth, and holding it gently between his teeth, runs out of the cave and away like lightning!
The fisherman, furious at having a fish snatched from his hand that he would so gladly have eaten, tried to chase the dog; but after a few steps he had a fit of coughing and had to turn back.
Meanwhile, when Alidoro found the little path leading to the town, he stopped and gently put his friend Pinocchio on the ground.
“How much I have to thank you for!” said the puppet.
“No need,” replied the dog, “you saved me, and what is done is repaid. As we know, everyone in this world must help one another.”
“But how did you happen to come to that cave?”

“I was still lying here on the beach, more dead than alive, when the wind brought me the smell of frying fish from far away. That smell made me hungry, and I followed it. If I’d arrived a minute later!…”
“Don’t say it!” cried Pinocchio, still shaking with fear. “Don’t say it! If you’d arrived a minute later, by now I’d have been fried, eaten, and digested. Brrr! I shiver just thinking about it!…”
Laughing, Alidoro held out his right paw to the puppet, who shook it very, very firmly as a sign of great friendship: and then they parted.
The dog took the road home: and Pinocchio, left alone, went to a hut nearby and asked a little old man who stood at the door warming himself in the sun:
“Tell me, good sir, do you know anything about a poor boy who was hurt in the head and was called Eugenio?”
“Some fishermen brought the boy to this hut, and now…”
“Now he must be dead!” Pinocchio interrupted in great sorrow.
“No: he’s alive now, and he’s already gone home.”
“Really?… Really?…” cried the puppet, jumping for joy. “So the wound wasn’t serious?…”
“But it could have been very serious, even deadly,” answered the old man, “because someone threw a large cardboard-bound book at his head.”
“And who threw it?”
“A schoolmate of his: someone called Pinocchio…”
“And who is this Pinocchio?” asked the puppet, pretending not to know.
“They say he’s a bad boy, a loafer, a real troublemaker.”
“Lies! All lies!”
“Do you know this Pinocchio?”
“By sight!” answered the puppet.
“And what do you think of him?” the old man asked.
“He seems a very good boy to me, eager to study, obedient, loving towards his father and his family…”
As the puppet calmly reeled off all these lies, he touched his nose and noticed that it had grown more than a hand’s width. Then, frightened, he began to cry:

“Don’t believe all the good things I’ve told you about him, sir; because I know Pinocchio very well, and I too can assure you that he really is a bad boy, disobedient and lazy, and that instead of going to school, he goes off causing trouble with his friends!”
As soon as he had said these words, his nose grew shorter and returned to its natural size, just as it had been before.
“And why are you all white like that?” the old man suddenly asked him.
“Well… without noticing, I rubbed against a freshly whitewashed wall,” answered the puppet, ashamed to explain that he had been coated in flour like a fish to be fried in a pan.
“And what have you done with your jacket, your shorts, and your cap?”
“I met some thieves and they stripped me. Tell me, good old man, do you happen to have any little thing I could wear, just so I can go home?”
“My boy, as for clothes, I only have a little sack where I keep my lupin beans. If you want it, take it: there it is.”

Pinocchio did not need telling twice: he immediately took the empty lupin sack, and after cutting a little hole in the bottom and two holes in the sides with scissors, he slipped it on like a shirt. And dressed so lightly, he set off towards the town. But along the road he felt far from calm; indeed, he took one step forward and one step back, and talking to himself, he kept saying:

“How can I face my good little Fairy? What will she say when she sees me?… Will she forgive this second piece of mischief?… I bet she won’t forgive me!… Oh! She certainly won’t forgive me!… And it serves me right: because I’m a rascal who always promises to change, and never keeps his promise!”

By the time he reached the town, it was dark night; and because the weather was dreadful and the rain was pouring down in buckets, he went straight to the Fairy’s house, determined to knock on the door and be let in.

But when he got there, his courage failed him, and instead of knocking, he ran about twenty steps away. Then he went back to the door a second time and did nothing: then he went up a third time and still nothing: the fourth time, trembling, he took the iron knocker in his hand and gave a tiny knock.

He waited and waited, until at last, after half an hour, a window opened on the top floor (the house had four storeys), and Pinocchio saw a large Snail lean out, with a little light burning on her head, and she said:
“Who is it at this hour?”
“Is the Fairy at home?” asked the puppet.
“The Fairy is asleep and doesn’t want to be woken: but who are you?”
“It’s me!”
“Who is me?”
“Pinocchio.”
“Who is Pinocchio?”
“The puppet, the one who lives with the Fairy.”
“Ah! I see,” said the Snail. “Wait there for me, and I’ll come down and open the door at once.”
“Hurry, please, because I’m dying of cold.”
“My boy, I’m a Snail, and Snails are never in a hurry.”
Meanwhile an hour passed, then two, and the door did not open: so Pinocchio, shaking with cold, fear, and the water soaking him, plucked up courage and knocked a second time, and knocked harder.
At that second knock, a window on the floor below opened, and the same Snail leaned out.
“Dear little Snail,” Pinocchio called from the street, “I’ve been waiting for two hours! And two hours on a terrible night like this are longer than two years. Hurry, please.”
“My boy,” that little creature answered from the window, perfectly calm and unhurried, “my boy, I’m a Snail, and Snails are never in a hurry.” And the window closed again.
Soon midnight struck: then one o’clock, then two o’clock, and the door was still shut.

Then Pinocchio lost his patience and angrily grabbed the door knocker to give a knock that would echo through the whole house; but the iron knocker suddenly turned into a living eel, which slipped from his hands and disappeared into a little stream of water flowing down the middle of the street.
“Oh, is that so?” cried Pinocchio, more and more blinded by anger. “If the knocker’s gone, I’ll keep knocking with my feet.”

And stepping back a little, he gave the house door a mighty kick. The blow was so hard that his foot went halfway into the wood: and when the puppet tried to pull it out again, all his efforts were useless, because the foot was stuck fast inside, like a nail hammered over at the end.
Imagine poor Pinocchio! He had to spend the rest of the night with one foot on the ground and the other in the air.

At dawn next morning the door finally opened. That good little creature the Snail had taken only nine hours to come down from the fourth floor to the street door. She really must have worked up a sweat.
“What are you doing with that foot stuck in the door?” she asked the puppet, laughing.
“It was an accident. Please see, dear little Snail, if you can free me from this misery.”
“My boy, that needs a carpenter, and I’ve never been a carpenter.”
“Ask the Fairy for me!”
“The Fairy is asleep and doesn’t want to be woken.”
“But what do you expect me to do, nailed to this door all day?”
“Amuse yourself by counting the ants passing along the street.”
“At least bring me something to eat, because I feel completely worn out.”
“At once!” said the Snail.
Sure enough, three and a half hours later, Pinocchio saw her return with a silver tray on her head. On the tray were a loaf of bread, a roast chicken, and four ripe apricots.
“Here is the breakfast the Fairy sends you,” said the Snail.

At the sight of that lovely food, the puppet felt comforted all over. But how disappointed he was when, on starting to eat, he discovered that the bread was made of plaster, the chicken of cardboard, and the four apricots of alabaster stone, coloured to look real.

He wanted to cry, he wanted to despair, he wanted to throw away the tray and everything on it; but instead, whether from great sorrow or the terrible emptiness in his stomach, the fact is that he fainted.
When he came round, he found himself lying on a sofa, with the Fairy beside him.
“I forgive you this time too,” the Fairy told him, “but you’ll be sorry if you play another of your tricks on me!”

Pinocchio promised and swore that he would study and always behave well. And he kept his word for the rest of the year. In fact, in the exams before the holidays, he had the honour of being the best in the school; and his behaviour in general was judged so good and pleasing that the Fairy, full of happiness, told him:
“Tomorrow, at last, your wish will come true!”
“What do you mean?”
“Tomorrow you will stop being a wooden puppet and become a good boy.”

Anyone who did not see Pinocchio’s joy at this longed-for news could never imagine it. All his friends and schoolmates were to be invited to a grand breakfast at the Fairy’s house the next day, to celebrate the great event together: and the Fairy had ordered two hundred cups of milky coffee and four hundred little rolls buttered inside and out. It promised to be a lovely, happy day: but…
Unfortunately, in the lives of puppets, there is always a “but” that spoils everything.
chapters.title: He returns to the Fairy’s house, and she promises that the next day he will no longer be a puppet but will become a boy. A grand breakfast of milky coffee is planned to celebrate this great event.

paragraphs: Naturally, Pinocchio immediately asked the Fairy’s permission to go around town inviting his friends: and the Fairy said:
“Go and invite your friends to tomorrow’s breakfast: but remember to come home before dark. Do you understand?”
“I promise I’ll be back within an hour,” replied the puppet.
“Be careful, Pinocchio! Children are quick to make promises, but most of the time they are slow to keep them.”
“But I’m not like the others: when I say something, I keep my word.”
“We shall see. If you disobey, it will be the worse for you.”
“Why?”
“Because children who don’t listen to advice from those who know more than they do always run into trouble.”
“And I’ve found that out!” said Pinocchio. “But I won’t make that mistake again!”
“We shall see whether you mean it.”
Without another word, the puppet said goodbye to his kind Fairy, who was rather like a mother to him, and went out of the house singing and dancing.

In just over an hour, all his friends had been invited. Some accepted at once and very gladly, while others needed a little persuading at first; but when they heard that the rolls for dipping in their milky coffee would be buttered on the outside too, they all ended up saying: “We’ll come too, to make you happy.”

Now you should know that among his friends and schoolmates, Pinocchio had one special, very dear friend whose name was Romeo; but everyone called him Candlewick, because his little body was thin, dry and lanky, just like the fresh wick of a night-light.

Candlewick was the laziest and naughtiest boy in the whole school: but Pinocchio loved him dearly. In fact, he went straight to his house to invite him to breakfast, and didn’t find him: he went back a second time, and Candlewick wasn’t there: he went back a third time, and made the journey for nothing.
Where could he find him? He searched here and searched there, until at last he spotted him hiding under the porch of a farmhouse.
“What are you doing there?” Pinocchio asked, coming closer.
“Waiting until midnight, to leave…”
“Where are you going?”
“Far, far, far away!”
“And I’ve been to your house three times looking for you!…”
“What did you want with me?”
“Haven’t you heard the big news? Don’t you know what good luck I’ve had?”
“What?”
“Tomorrow I’ll stop being a puppet and become a boy like you and everyone else.”
“Good luck to you.”
“So I’ll expect you at my house for breakfast tomorrow.”
“But I’m telling you I’m leaving tonight.”
“At what time?”
“Soon.”
“And where are you going?”
“To live in a country… that’s the best country in the world: a real paradise!…”
“And what is it called?”
“It’s called the Land of Toys. Why don’t you come too?”
“Me? Certainly not!”

“You’re wrong, Pinocchio! Believe me, you’ll regret it if you don’t come. Where could you find a better country for us boys? There are no schools there: there are no teachers there; there are no books there. In that wonderful country, nobody ever studies. There’s no school on Thursdays: and every week has six Thursdays and one Sunday. Just imagine, the autumn holidays begin on the first of January and end on the last of December. That’s the sort of country I really like! That’s how every properly run country ought to be!…”
“But how do people spend their days in the Land of Toys?”
“They spend them playing and having fun from morning till night. Then in the evening they go to bed, and the next morning they start all over again. What do you think?”
“Hmm!…” said Pinocchio; and he gave his head a little shake, as if to say: “I’d quite like to live that way myself.”
“So, will you come with me? Yes or no? Make up your mind.”

“No, no, no, and no again. I’ve promised my kind Fairy to become a good boy now, and I mean to keep my promise. In fact, as I can see the sun going down, I’ll leave you straight away and run home. So goodbye, and have a good journey.”
“Where are you rushing off to in such a hurry?”
“Home. My kind Fairy wants me back before dark.”
“Wait another two minutes.”
“I’ll be too late.”
“Just two minutes.”
“And what if the Fairy scolds me?”
“Let her scold. Once she’s had a good shout, she’ll calm down,” said that rascal Candlewick.
“And how are you going? Alone or with others?”
“Alone? There’ll be more than a hundred boys.”
“And are you travelling on foot?”
“The wagon that’s picking me up and taking me right into that wonderfully lucky country will be coming along here soon.”
“What wouldn’t I give for the wagon to come now!…”
“Why?”
“To see you all leave together.”
“Stay here a little longer and you will.”
“No, no: I want to go home.”
“Wait another two minutes.”
“I’ve waited far too long already. The Fairy will be worrying about me.”
“Poor Fairy! Is she afraid the bats will eat you?”
“But tell me,” Pinocchio went on, “are you really sure there aren’t any schools at all in that country?…”
“Not a sign of one.”
“And no teachers either?”
“Not a single one.”
“And you never have to study?”
“Never, never, never!”
“What a wonderful country!” said Pinocchio, his mouth beginning to water. “What a wonderful country! I’ve never been there, but I can picture it!…”
“Why don’t you come too?”
“There’s no point tempting me! I’ve promised my kind Fairy to become a sensible boy now, and I won’t break my word.”
“Then goodbye, and give my very best wishes to the grammar schools!… And the upper schools too, if you meet them on the way.”
“Goodbye, Candlewick; have a good journey, enjoy yourself, and remember your friends sometimes.”
With that, the puppet took two steps as if to leave: but then he stopped, turned to his friend and asked:
“But are you quite sure that every week in that country has six Thursdays and one Sunday?”
“Quite sure.”
“But do you know for certain that the holidays begin on the first of January and end on the last of December?”
“Absolutely certain.”
“What a wonderful country!” Pinocchio repeated, spitting with sheer delight. Then, making up his mind, he added in a great hurry:
“So, goodbye for real: and have a good journey.”
“Goodbye.”
