“How soon will you leave?”
“Soon.”
“What a pity! If you were leaving in just an hour, I might almost be able to wait.”
“And the Fairy?”
“I’m late already!… And getting home an hour earlier or an hour later makes no difference.”
“Poor Pinocchio! And what if the Fairy scolds you?”
“Never mind! I’ll let her scold. Once she’s had a good shout, she’ll calm down.”

Meanwhile night had fallen, and it was quite dark: when suddenly they saw a little light moving in the distance… and heard the jingle of bells and a trumpet call, so small and muffled that it sounded like a mosquito’s whine.
“There it is!” shouted Candlewick, jumping to his feet.
“What is it?” Pinocchio asked quietly.
“It’s the wagon coming to pick me up. So, are you coming, yes or no?”
“But is it really true,” the puppet asked, “that children in that country never have to study?”
“Never, never, never!”
“What a wonderful country!… What a wonderful country!… What a wonderful country!…”
chapters.title: Instead of becoming a boy, Pinocchio secretly leaves with his friend Candlewick for the Land of Toys.

paragraphs: At last the wagon arrived: and it arrived without the slightest noise, because its wheels were wrapped in loose plant fibres and rags.
It was pulled by twelve pairs of little donkeys, all the same size, but with different coats.
Some were grey, others white, others speckled like salt and pepper, and others marked with broad yellow and blue stripes.

But the strangest thing was this: those twelve pairs, or twenty-four little donkeys, instead of wearing horseshoes like all the other animals that pulled or carried loads, wore little men’s boots made of white leather.
And the driver of the wagon?…

Picture a little man wider than he was tall, soft and oily as a ball of butter, with a little rosy-apple face, a tiny mouth that was always smiling and a soft, sweet voice like a cat appealing to the kind heart of the lady of the house.

As soon as children saw him, they were all delighted with him and raced each other to climb onto his wagon, so he could take them to that true paradise known on the map by the tempting name of the Land of Toys.

Indeed, the wagon was already packed with boys between eight and twelve years old, piled on top of one another like anchovies in salty water. They were uncomfortable, they were squashed, they could hardly breathe: but nobody said “ow!” and nobody complained. The happy thought that in a few hours they would reach a country with no books, schools or teachers made them so pleased and willing to put up with things that they felt neither discomfort nor jolts, hunger, thirst or sleepiness.
As soon as the wagon stopped, the little man turned to Candlewick and, with a thousand little faces and gestures, asked him with a smile:
“Tell me, my handsome boy, would you like to come to that happy country too?”
“Of course I would!”
“But I must warn you, my dear, there’s no room left in the wagon. As you can see, it’s full!…”
“Never mind!” Candlewick replied. “If there’s no room inside, I’ll manage sitting on the wagon shafts.” And with a leap, he sat astride the long poles at the front.
“And you, my love,” said the little man, turning to Pinocchio with great politeness, “what do you intend to do? Are you coming with us or staying?…”
“I’m staying,” answered Pinocchio. “I want to go home: I want to study and do well at school, like all good boys.”
“Good luck to you!”
“Pinocchio,” said Candlewick then, “listen to me: come with us and we’ll have fun!”
“No, no, no!”
“Come with us and we’ll have fun!” shouted four more voices from inside the wagon.
“Come with us and we’ll have fun!” a hundred voices yelled together.
“And if I come with you, what will my kind Fairy say?” asked the puppet, who was beginning to soften and change his mind.
“Don’t fill your head with so many worries. Remember, we’re going to a country where we’ll be free to make a racket from morning till night!”
Pinocchio didn’t answer, but gave a sigh; then he gave another sigh: then a third sigh: at last he said:
“Make a little room for me: I want to come too!…”
“All the places are taken,” replied the little man, “but to show you how welcome you are, I can give you my seat on the driver’s box.”
“And what about you?”
“I’ll walk.”
“Certainly not, I won’t allow it. I’d rather climb onto the back of one of these little donkeys!” cried Pinocchio.

No sooner said than done, he went up to the right-hand donkey in the first pair and made to climb onto its back: but the little animal turned sharply, gave him a great butt in the stomach and knocked him head over heels.
Just imagine the rude, wild burst of laughter from all the boys watching.
But the little man did not laugh. He went up to the stubborn little donkey very lovingly and, pretending to kiss it, bit off half its right ear.

Meanwhile Pinocchio, getting up from the ground in a fury, sprang onto the poor animal’s back. And it was such a splendid leap that the boys stopped laughing and began to shout, “Hooray for Pinocchio!” and clap their hands without stopping.
Then suddenly the little donkey raised both its back legs and gave such a mighty buck that it flung the poor puppet into the middle of the road, onto a heap of gravel.

There was another great burst of laughter: but instead of laughing, the little man felt so much love for the restless donkey that, with a kiss, he took off half its other ear. Then he said to the puppet:
“Climb back on, and don’t be afraid. That little donkey had some silly ideas in its head: but I’ve whispered a word or two in its ears, and I hope I’ve made it gentle and sensible.”

Pinocchio climbed on, and the wagon began to move: but as the donkeys galloped and the wagon raced over the stones of the main road, the puppet thought he heard a low voice, so faint he could barely make it out, saying:
“Poor fool! You insisted on having your own way, but you’ll regret it!”

Almost frightened, Pinocchio looked around to see where these words came from; but he saw no one: the donkeys galloped, the wagon raced along, the boys inside it slept, Candlewick snored like a dormouse, and the little man on the driver’s box hummed under his breath:
“Everyone sleeps at night, But I never sleep…”
After another half-kilometre, Pinocchio heard the faint little voice say:

“Remember this, little fool! Boys who stop studying and turn their backs on books, schools and teachers, to spend all their time playing and having fun, can only come to a bad end! I know from experience, and I can tell you!… One day you’ll cry too, as I’m crying today… but then it will be too late!…”
At these softly whispered words, the puppet, more frightened than ever, jumped down from his mount and went to hold his little donkey by the muzzle.
And imagine how he felt when he discovered that his little donkey was crying… and crying just like a boy!
“Hey, little gentleman,” Pinocchio shouted to the owner of the wagon, “do you know what’s happening? This little donkey is crying.”
“Let him cry: he’ll laugh on his wedding day!”
“But have you taught him to talk as well?”
“No: he learned to mumble a few words by himself, after spending three years with a group of trained dogs.”
“Poor animal!…”
“Come, come…” said the little man, “let’s not waste our time watching a donkey cry. Climb back on, and let’s go: the night is cool, and the road is long.”
Pinocchio obeyed without a word. The wagon set off again: and at dawn they arrived safely in the Land of Toys.

This country was like no other country in the world. Its people were all boys. The oldest were fourteen: the youngest were barely eight. In the streets there was enough joy, noise and shouting to drive you out of your mind! Gangs of boys everywhere: some played with nuts, some with throwing tiles, some with balls, some rode bicycles, some rode little wooden horses: these played blind man’s buff; those chased each other: others, dressed as clowns, swallowed burning plant fibres: some acted, some sang, some did somersaults, some amused themselves walking on their hands with their legs in the air: some rolled hoops, some marched around dressed as generals with paper helmets and papier-mâché swords: some laughed, some yelled, some called, some clapped, some whistled, some copied the sound of a hen that has laid an egg: in short, there was such chaos, such chatter, such a wild racket that you had to put cotton wool in your ears to keep from being deafened. In every square stood little canvas theatres, packed with boys from morning till night, and on all the walls you could read lovely things written in charcoal, like these: “Hooray for toyz!” instead of “toys”; “We dont wont skools” instead of “We don’t want schools”; “Down with arithmatick” instead of “arithmetic”, and other fine examples like them.

As soon as Pinocchio, Candlewick and all the other boys who had travelled with the little man set foot in the town, they plunged straight into the great uproar, and within minutes, as you can easily imagine, they were everyone’s friends. Who could be happier, who could be more pleased than they were? With endless games and all kinds of fun, the hours, days and weeks passed like flashes of lightning.
“Oh, what a wonderful life!” Pinocchio said whenever he happened to run into Candlewick.

“So you see I was right?” the other replied. “And to think you didn’t want to come! To think you’d got it into your head to go home to your Fairy and waste your time studying! If you’re free today from the boredom of books and school, you owe it to me, my advice and my care for you, don’t you agree? Only true friends know how to do such great favours.”

“It’s true, Candlewick! If I’m a really happy boy today, it’s all thanks to you. And do you know what the teacher used to say about you? He was always telling me: ‘Don’t spend time with that rascal Candlewick, because Candlewick is a bad friend, and he can only advise you to do wrong!…’”
“Poor teacher!” the other replied, shaking his head. “I know only too well that he couldn’t stand me and always enjoyed telling lies about me; but I’m generous, and I forgive him!”
“What a noble heart!” said Pinocchio, hugging his friend lovingly and kissing him between the eyes.

By now this wonderful life of playing and having fun all day, without ever seeing a book or a school, had lasted five months; when one morning Pinocchio woke up and got, as people say, a very nasty surprise, which put him in a thoroughly bad mood.
chapters.title: After five months of easy living, Pinocchio is amazed to find a fine pair of donkey ears growing, and becomes a little donkey, tail and all.

paragraphs: And what was this surprise?
I’ll tell you, my dear young readers: the surprise was that when Pinocchio woke up, he naturally happened to scratch his head; and as he scratched his head, he discovered…
Can you guess what he discovered?
To his enormous surprise, he discovered that his ears had grown by more than a hand’s width.

You know that from the day he was made, the puppet had tiny, tiny ears: so tiny that you couldn’t even see them with your bare eyes! So imagine how he felt when his own hands told him that during the night his ears had grown so long that they looked like two brushes made of reeds. He immediately looked for a mirror to see himself: but finding no mirror, he filled his washbasin with water and, looking into it, saw what he would never have wanted to see: he saw his own face decorated with a magnificent pair of donkey ears. I’ll leave you to imagine poor Pinocchio’s pain, shame and despair!
He began to cry, to scream, to bang his head against the wall: but the more upset he became, the more his ears grew, grew, grew, and became hairy at the tips.
At the sound of those piercing cries, a pretty little Marmot who lived upstairs came into the room: and seeing the puppet so terribly upset, she asked with concern:
“What’s wrong, my dear neighbour?”
“I’m ill, my little Marmot, very ill… and I’ve got an illness that frightens me! Do you know how to take a pulse?”
“A little.”
“Then feel mine and see whether I have a fever.”
The little Marmot raised her right front paw: and after feeling Pinocchio’s pulse, she sighed and said:
“My friend, I’m sorry to have to give you bad news!…”
“What is it?”
“You have a very nasty fever!”
“And what sort of fever is it?”
“Donkey fever.”
“I don’t understand that fever!” replied the puppet, who understood it only too well.
“Then I’ll explain it,” the little Marmot went on; “you should know that in two or three hours you’ll no longer be either a puppet or a boy…”
“And what will I be?”
“In two or three hours you’ll become a real little donkey, like the ones that pull carts and carry cabbages and lettuce to market.”
“Oh, poor me! Poor me!” cried Pinocchio, grabbing both his ears and furiously pulling and tearing at them, as if they belonged to someone else.

“My dear,” the little Marmot replied to comfort him, “what can you do about it? It’s your fate now, it’s written in the laws of wisdom that all those lazy boys who grow tired of books, schools and teachers, and spend their days playing with toys, games and amusements, must sooner or later turn into little donkeys.”
“But is that really true?” asked the puppet, sobbing.
“Sadly, it is! And crying is no use now. You should have thought of it before!”
“But it isn’t my fault: believe me, little Marmot, it’s all Candlewick’s fault!…”
“And who is this Candlewick?”

“A schoolmate of mine. I wanted to go home: I wanted to be good: I wanted to keep studying and do well… but Candlewick said to me: ‘Why do you want to bore yourself studying? Why do you want to go to school?… Come with me to the Land of Toys instead: we won’t study there any more; we’ll have fun from morning till night and always be happy.’”
“And why did you follow the advice of that false friend, that bad companion?”

“Why?… Because, my little Marmot, I’m a puppet with no sense… and no heart. Oh! If I’d had even the tiniest bit of heart, I’d never have left that kind Fairy who loved me like a mother and had done so much for me!… And by now I wouldn’t be a puppet any more… I’d be a good little boy instead, like so many others! Oh!… But if I meet Candlewick, he’d better watch out! I’ll give him a good telling-off.”

And he made to go out. But when he reached the door, he remembered his donkey ears, and, ashamed to show them in public, what did he think of? He took a large cotton cap, put it on his head and pulled it down below his ears.

Then he went out and began searching everywhere for Candlewick. He looked in the streets, in the squares, in the little theatres, everywhere: but he couldn’t find him. He asked everyone he met along the way about him, but nobody had seen him.
Then he went to look for him at home: and when he reached the door, he knocked.
“Who’s there?” Candlewick asked from inside.
“It’s me!” the puppet replied.
“Wait a little, and I’ll open the door.”
Half an hour later, the door opened: and imagine how Pinocchio felt when he went into the room and saw his friend Candlewick wearing a large cotton cap pulled down below his nose.
The sight of that cap almost cheered Pinocchio up, and he immediately thought:
“Could my friend have the same illness as me? Could he have donkey fever too?…”
And pretending not to have noticed anything, he asked with a smile:
“How are you, my dear Candlewick?”
“Very well: like a mouse in a wheel of Parmesan cheese.”
“Do you really mean that?”
“And why should I tell you a lie?”
“Excuse me, my friend: then why are you wearing that cotton cap that covers both your ears?”
“The doctor told me to, because I’ve hurt my knee. And why are you, dear Pinocchio, wearing your cotton cap pulled down below your ears?”
“The doctor told me to, because I’ve scraped my foot.”
“Oh, poor Pinocchio!”
“Oh, poor Candlewick!…”
These words were followed by a very long silence, during which the two friends did nothing but look at each other mockingly.
At last the puppet said to his friend in a little voice as sweet and smooth as a flute:
“Tell me something, my dear Candlewick: have you ever had trouble with your ears?”
“Never!… Have you?”
“Never! Still, since this morning, one of my ears has been hurting terribly.”
“I’ve got the same trouble.”
“You too?… And which ear hurts?”
“Both of them. And yours?”
“Both of them. Could it be the same illness?”
“I’m afraid so.”
“Will you do me a favour, Candlewick?”
“Gladly! With all my heart.”
“Will you show me your ears?”
“Why not? But I want to see yours first, dear Pinocchio.”
“No: you must go first.”
“No, my dear! You first and then me!”
“Well,” said the puppet then, “let’s make a deal as good friends.”
“Let’s hear the deal.”
“Let’s both take off our caps at the same time: agreed?”
“Agreed.”
“Then get ready!”
And Pinocchio began counting aloud:
“One! Two! Three!”
At the word “three!” the two boys took their caps off and threw them into the air.

And then something happened that would seem unbelievable if it weren’t true. When Pinocchio and Candlewick saw that the same disaster had struck them both, instead of feeling ashamed and sad, they began winking at each other’s enormously overgrown ears, and after all sorts of silly behaviour, they burst out laughing.

And they laughed, laughed, laughed until they had to hold their stomachs: but just as they were laughing hardest, Candlewick suddenly fell silent and, staggering and changing colour, said to his friend:
“Help, help, Pinocchio!”
“What’s wrong?”
“Oh dear! I can’t stand on my legs any more.”
“Neither can I!” cried Pinocchio, weeping and wobbling.

And as they said this, they both sank onto all fours and began to move and run around the room on their hands and feet. And as they ran, their arms turned into legs, their faces grew long and became muzzles, and their backs were covered with light grey fur speckled with black.

But do you know when the worst moment came for those two unlucky creatures? The worst and most shameful moment was when they felt tails growing behind them. Overcome with shame and misery, they tried to cry and complain about their fate.
If only they hadn’t! Instead of moans and complaints, they let out donkey brays: and braying loudly together, they both went, “Hee-haw, hee-haw, hee-haw.”
Just then there was a knock at the door, and a voice outside said:
“Open up! It’s the little man, the driver of the wagon that brought you to this country. Open up at once, or you’ll be sorry!”
chapters.title: Pinocchio grows donkey ears, then becomes a real little donkey and starts to bray.

paragraphs: Seeing that the door wasn’t opening, the little man kicked it wide open with a tremendous blow: and coming into the room, he said to Pinocchio and Candlewick with his usual little smile:
“Well done, boys! You brayed beautifully; I recognised your voices at once, and that’s why I’m here.”
At these words, the two little donkeys stood sadly with their heads down, their ears drooping and their tails between their legs.
First the little man stroked them, patted them and felt them all over: then he took out a grooming comb and began to give them a good brushing.
And when he had brushed them until they shone like two mirrors, he put ropes around their heads and led them to the market square, hoping to sell them and make a tidy profit.

And indeed, buyers were not long in coming. Candlewick was bought by a farmer whose donkey had died the day before, and Pinocchio was sold to the Director of a company of clowns and rope-dancers, who bought him to train him and then make him jump and dance with the company’s other animals.

And now, my young readers, do you understand what a fine trade the little man carried on? This horrible little monster, who looked all sweetness and kindness, would go around the world with a wagon from time to time; on the way, with promises and sweet words, he collected all the lazy boys who were tired of books and school; and after loading them onto his wagon, he took them to the Land of Toys to spend all their time playing, making noise and having fun. Then, when those poor, fooled boys had turned into little donkeys from always playing and never studying, he happily took possession of them and brought them to fairs and markets to sell. And in this way, within a few years, he had made piles of money and become a millionaire.
I don’t know what happened to Candlewick: but I do know that from the very first days, Pinocchio faced a very hard life of rough treatment.
When he was led into the stable, his new master filled the feeding trough with straw: but after tasting a mouthful, Pinocchio spat it out.
Then, grumbling, his master filled the trough with hay: but he didn’t like hay either.
“Ah! You don’t like hay either?” his master shouted angrily. “Just you wait, my pretty donkey: if you’ve got fussy ideas in your head, I’ll knock them out of you!…”
And to teach him a lesson, he immediately struck him across the legs with a whip.
The pain made Pinocchio cry and bray, and as he brayed he said:
“Hee-haw, hee-haw, I can’t digest straw!…”
“Then eat hay!” replied his master, who understood donkey language perfectly.
“Hee-haw, hee-haw, hay gives me a stomach ache!…”
“So you expect me to feed a donkey like you on chicken breasts and stuffed chicken in jelly?” his master added, growing angrier and giving him a second stroke of the whip.
At that second stroke, Pinocchio wisely fell silent at once and said no more.
Meanwhile the stable was shut, and Pinocchio was left alone: and because he hadn’t eaten for many hours, he began yawning with hunger. And as he yawned, he opened a mouth as wide as an oven.
At last, finding nothing else in the trough, he gave in and chewed some hay; and after chewing it thoroughly, he shut his eyes and swallowed it.

“This hay isn’t bad,” he said to himself then; “but how much better it would have been if I’d kept on studying!… By now, instead of hay, I could be eating a crust of fresh bread and a nice slice of salami. Never mind!…”
The next morning, when he woke, he immediately looked in the trough for more hay: but there was none, because he had eaten it all during the night.
Then he took a mouthful of chopped straw: and as he chewed it, he had to admit that chopped straw tasted nothing like Milan-style risotto or Naples-style macaroni.
“Never mind!” he repeated, still chewing. “May my misfortune at least be a lesson to all the disobedient boys who don’t want to study. Never mind!… Never mind!”

“Never mind, indeed!” shouted his master, coming into the stable just then. “Do you think, my pretty donkey, that I bought you just to give you food and drink? I bought you to work and earn me lots of money. Come on, then, be good! Come into the Circus with me, and there I’ll teach you to jump through hoops, break through paper barrels with your head and dance the waltz and the polka standing on your back legs.”
Poor Pinocchio, whether he liked it or not, had to learn all these wonderful things; but learning them took three months of lessons and many lashes hard enough to strip his fur.
At last the day came when his master could announce a truly amazing show. The coloured posters stuck on street corners said:
“GRAND GALA SHOW”
“This evening THERE WILL BE THE USUAL AMAZING LEAPS AND EXERCISES PERFORMED BY ALL THE ARTISTS and all the male and female horses of the Company, and also”
“Appearing for the first time, the famous”
“LITTLE DONKEY PINOCCHIO”
“known as THE STAR OF THE DANCE”
“The theatre will be as bright as day”
That evening, as you can imagine, the theatre was packed an hour before the show began.
There wasn’t a single armchair, reserved seat or box left, not even if you paid its weight in gold.
The Circus benches were swarming with boys and girls of every age, almost feverish with excitement to see the famous little donkey Pinocchio dance.

When the first part of the show was over, the Director of the company, wearing a black coat, tight white trousers and leather boots reaching above his knees, appeared before the huge audience and, making a deep bow, solemnly gave the following muddled speech:
“Respectable public, gentlemen and ladies!”

“As the humble undersigned, being on my way through this famous metropoli-train, I wished to reproduce for myself the honour and also the pleasure of presenting to this clever and large audience a famous little donkey, who has already had the honour of dancing before His Majesty the Emperor of all the main courts of Europe.”
“And with thanking you, help us with your lively presence and excuse us!”

This speech was greeted with much laughter and applause: but the applause doubled and became a kind of hurricane when the little donkey Pinocchio appeared in the middle of the Circus. He was dressed in all his finery. He had a new shiny leather bridle with brass buckles and studs; two white camellia flowers by his ears: his mane was divided into curls tied with little red silk bows: a broad gold and silver sash crossed his waist, and his tail was woven with dark red and sky-blue velvet ribbons. In short, he was a little donkey anyone could fall in love with!
As he presented him to the public, the Director added these words:

“My respectable listeners! I shall not tell you lies of the great difficulties I have squashed to understand and master this mammal, while he grazed freely from mountain to mountain on the plains of the burning zone. Please notice how much wild game pours from his eyes, for as every means of taming him to the life of well-behaved four-legged creatures proved vain and vain-looking, I have often had to turn to the friendly language of the whip. But each kindness, instead of making him love me, made him more badly minded towards me. Yet, following the system of Galles, I found in his skull a small bony Carthage, which the Medical Faculty of Paris itself recognised as the bulb that regrows hair and war-dancing. And that is why I decided to train him in dancing, and also the related jumping through hoops and paper-lined barrels. Admire him, and then judge him! But before I take my brother-in-law of you, allow me, gentlemen, to invite you to tomorrow evening’s daytime show: but in the glorious event that rainy weather threatens water, the show, instead of tomorrow evening, will be postponed to tomorrow morning, at eleven a.m. in the afternoon.”
Here the Director made another very deep bow: then, turning to Pinocchio, he said:
“Come on, Pinocchio! Before beginning your exercises, greet this respectable public, gentlemen, ladies and children!”
Pinocchio obediently bent both his front knees at once and remained kneeling until the Director cracked his whip and shouted:
“Walk!”
Then the little donkey stood on all four legs and began to go around the Circus at a walk.
After a little while, the Director shouted:
“Trot!” And Pinocchio obeyed the command and changed from walking to trotting.
“Gallop!” And Pinocchio began to gallop.
“Full speed!” And Pinocchio began to run as fast as he could. But as he raced like a racehorse, the Director raised his arm and fired a pistol into the air.
At the shot, the little donkey pretended to be wounded and fell flat in the Circus, as though he were truly dying.

Getting up amid a burst of applause, shouting and clapping that rose to the skies, he naturally lifted his head and looked up… and as he looked, he saw a beautiful lady in a box, wearing a heavy gold necklace with a locket hanging from it. Painted inside the locket was a picture of a puppet.
“That picture is me!… That lady is the Fairy!” Pinocchio said to himself, recognising her at once: and overcome with happiness, he tried to cry out:
“Oh, my dear Fairy! Oh, my dear Fairy!”
But instead of these words, such a loud, long bray came out of his throat that it made all the audience laugh, especially all the children in the theatre.
Then the Director, to teach him and make him understand that braying in the public’s face was bad manners, struck him on the nose with the handle of his whip.
The poor little donkey stuck out a hand’s length of tongue and licked his nose for at least five minutes, perhaps thinking he could wipe away the pain he had felt.
But how desperate he was when he looked up a second time and saw that the box was empty and the Fairy had vanished!…
He felt as though he were dying: his eyes filled with tears, and he began to cry bitterly. But nobody noticed, least of all the Director, who cracked his whip instead and shouted:
“Be good, Pinocchio! Now you’ll show these ladies and gentlemen how gracefully you can jump through hoops.”

Pinocchio tried two or three times: but whenever he reached the hoop, instead of going through it, he took the easier way underneath. At last he leaped and went through: but unfortunately his back legs caught in the hoop, so that he landed in a heap on the other side.
When he got up, he was lame and could hardly make his way back to the stable.
“Bring out Pinocchio! We want the little donkey! Bring out the little donkey!” the children shouted from the seats, feeling sorry for him and upset by the sad accident.
But the little donkey did not appear again that evening.
The next morning the vet, the doctor for animals, examined him and said he would be lame for the rest of his life.
Then the Director said to his stable boy:
“What use is a lame donkey to me? He’d just eat at my expense for nothing. Take him to the square and sell him again.”
When they reached the square, they soon found a buyer, who asked the stable boy:
“How much do you want for that lame little donkey?”
“Twenty lire.”
“I’ll give you twenty soldi. Don’t think I’m buying him to use him: I’m only buying him for his skin. I can see his skin is very tough, and I want to make a drum with it for my village band.”
I’ll leave you, children, to imagine how delighted poor Pinocchio was when he heard that he was going to become a drum!

The fact is that as soon as the buyer had paid his twenty soldi, he led the little donkey onto a rock by the sea; and putting a stone around his neck and tying one of his legs to a rope he held in his hand, he suddenly gave him a shove and pushed him into the water.

With that heavy stone around his neck, Pinocchio sank at once; and the buyer, still holding the rope tightly, sat on the rock and waited until the little donkey had had plenty of time to drown, so that he could then strip off his skin.
chapters.title: Now a real little donkey, he is taken to be sold, and the Director of a company of clowns buys him to teach him to dance and jump through hoops: but one evening he becomes lame, and another man buys him to make a drum from his skin.

paragraphs: After the little donkey had been underwater for fifty minutes, the buyer said to himself:
“By now my poor lame little donkey must be well and truly drowned. So let’s pull him up and make that fine drum out of his skin.”

And he began pulling the rope he had tied around its leg: and he pulled, pulled, pulled, until at last he saw something appear at the surface… Can you guess? Instead of a dead little donkey, a living puppet appeared at the surface, wriggling like an eel.
At the sight of that wooden puppet, the poor man thought he was dreaming, and stood there stunned, with his mouth open and his eyes bulging.
Recovering a little from his first surprise, he said, weeping and stammering:
“And where’s the little donkey I threw into the sea?…”
“I’m that little donkey!” the puppet answered, laughing.
“You?”
“Me.”
“Ah, you rascal! Are you trying to make fun of me?”
“Make fun of you? Not at all, dear master: I’m quite serious.”
“But how can you, who were a little donkey a moment ago, have become a wooden puppet while you were in the water?…”
“It must be the seawater. The sea plays tricks like that.”
“Watch out, puppet, watch out!… Don’t think you can have fun at my expense. You’ll be sorry if I lose my patience!”
“Well, master: do you want to hear the whole true story? Untie my leg and I’ll tell it to you.”
The buyer, that muddle-headed fellow, was curious to hear the true story and immediately untied the knot in the rope holding him: and then Pinocchio, as free as a bird in the air, began:

“You should know that I was a wooden puppet just as I am today: but I was on the very edge of becoming a boy, like so many in this world: except that, because I didn’t want to study and listened to bad friends, I ran away from home… and one fine day, when I woke, I found I’d turned into a donkey with great big ears… and a great big tail!… How ashamed I was!… Such shame, dear master, that may blessed Saint Anthony spare even you from ever feeling it! I was taken to the donkey market to be sold and bought by the Director of a company of horse performers, who got it into his head to make me a great dancer or hoop-jumper; but one evening, during the show, I had a nasty fall in the theatre and became lame in both legs. Then the Director, not knowing what to do with a lame donkey, sent me to be sold again, and you bought me!”
“Sadly, yes! And I paid twenty soldi for you. And now who’s going to give me back my poor twenty soldi?”
“And why did you buy me? You bought me to make a drum out of my skin!… A drum!…”
“Sadly, yes! And now where will I find another skin!…”
“Don’t despair, master. There are plenty of little donkeys in this world!”
“Tell me, you cheeky brat: does your story end there?”

“No,” the puppet replied, “just a few more words, and then it’s finished. After buying me, you brought me here to kill me, but then, giving in to a kind feeling of pity, you chose to tie a stone around my neck and throw me to the bottom of the sea instead. Such gentle feelings do you great credit, and I’ll be grateful to you for ever. However, dear master, this time you made your plans without considering the Fairy…”
“And who is this Fairy?”

“She’s my mother, and she’s like all those good mothers who love their children dearly and never take their eyes off them, and lovingly help them in every misfortune, even when those children, because of their foolishness and bad behaviour, deserve to be abandoned and left to look after themselves. So, as I was saying, as soon as the kind Fairy saw I was in danger of drowning, she sent an endless shoal of fish around me, and, thinking I really was a dead little donkey, they began to eat me! And what mouthfuls they took! I’d never have believed fish could be even greedier than children! Some ate my ears, some my muzzle, some my neck and mane, some the skin on my legs, some the fur on my back… and among them was one little fish so polite that he even kindly ate my tail.”
“From this day on,” the buyer said in horror, “I swear I won’t taste fish again. I’d be far too upset to cut open a fried mullet or hake and find a donkey’s tail inside!”

“I feel just the same,” the puppet replied, laughing. “Anyway, you should know that once the fish had finished eating all that donkey covering from my head to my feet, they naturally reached the bone… or rather, they reached the wood, because, as you can see, I’m made of very hard wood. But after their first bites, those greedy fish realised at once that wood wasn’t meat for their teeth, and disgusted by this food they couldn’t digest, they went off in all directions without even turning back to thank me… And that explains how, when you pulled up the rope, you found a live puppet instead of a dead little donkey.”

“I don’t care about your story!” the buyer shouted furiously. “I know I spent twenty soldi buying you, and I want my money back. Do you know what I’ll do? I’ll take you back to market and sell you by weight as dry wood for lighting a fire in the fireplace.”
“Go ahead and sell me: I don’t mind,” said Pinocchio. But as he said this, he leaped into the water. And swimming happily away from the shore, he shouted to the poor buyer:
“Goodbye, master; if you need a skin to make a drum, remember me.”
Then he laughed and swam on: and after a while, turning back, he shouted even louder:
“Goodbye, master;… if you need some dry wood to light your fireplace, remember me.”

In the blink of an eye, he was so far away that he was almost out of sight; or rather, all you could see on the sea was a tiny black dot, which now and then stuck its legs out of the water and tumbled and leaped like a dolphin in a good mood.

While Pinocchio was swimming wherever he pleased, he saw a rock in the middle of the sea that looked like white marble, and on top of the rock a pretty little Goat, who bleated lovingly and beckoned him closer.

The strangest thing was this: the little Goat’s coat, instead of being white or black or spotted with different colours like other goats’, was blue, and such a shining blue that it strongly reminded him of the beautiful Little Girl’s hair.

I’ll leave you to imagine whether poor Pinocchio’s heart began beating faster! With twice the strength and energy, he swam towards the white rock; and he was already halfway there when the horrible head of a sea monster rose out of the water and came towards him, with a mouth open like a huge pit and three rows of fangs that would have been frightening even in a picture.
And do you know who that sea monster was?
That sea monster was none other than the enormous Shark mentioned several times in this story, who, because of his killings and his endless hunger, was nicknamed “the Attila of fish and fishermen”.
Imagine poor Pinocchio’s terror at the sight of the monster. He tried to dodge it, to change direction: he tried to escape: but that enormous open mouth kept coming towards him as fast as an arrow.
“Hurry, Pinocchio, please!” bleated the pretty little Goat.
And Pinocchio swam desperately with his arms, his chest, his legs and his feet.
“Quick, Pinocchio, the monster’s getting closer!…”
And Pinocchio gathered all his strength and swam twice as hard.
“Look out, Pinocchio!… The monster’s catching you! There it is!… There it is!… Hurry, please, or you’re lost!…”

And Pinocchio swam faster than ever, on and on and on, as fast as a bullet. He was already nearing the rock, and the little Goat was leaning right out over the sea, holding out her front legs to help him out of the water… But!…

But now it was too late! The monster had caught up with him. Drawing in a breath, the monster sucked in the poor puppet as it might have swallowed a hen’s egg, and gulped him down so violently and greedily that Pinocchio, falling into the Shark’s body, landed with such a dreadful bump that he was stunned for a quarter of an hour.

When he came to his senses after that shock, he had no idea where in the world he was. All around him was darkness: darkness so black and deep that he felt he’d put his head into an inkwell full of ink. He listened and heard no sound; only now and then did great gusts of wind hit his face. At first he couldn’t understand where that wind came from: but then he realised it came from the monster’s lungs. For you should know that the Shark suffered badly from asthma, and when he breathed it was just like the north wind blowing.
At first Pinocchio tried to be brave: but when he had checked again and again that he was shut inside the sea monster’s body, he began to cry and scream; and as he cried he said:
“Help! Help! Oh, poor me! Isn’t there anyone coming to save me?”
“Who do you expect to save you, you poor thing?” said a cracked, harsh voice like an out-of-tune guitar in the darkness.
“Who’s speaking like that?” asked Pinocchio, feeling icy with fear.
“It’s me! I’m a poor Tuna, swallowed by the Shark along with you. And what kind of fish are you?”
“I’ve nothing to do with fish. I’m a puppet.”
“Then if you’re not a fish, why did you let the monster swallow you?”
“I didn’t let him swallow me: he’s the one who swallowed me! And now, what are we to do here in the dark?…”
“Accept it and wait until the Shark has digested us both!…”
“But I don’t want to be digested!” Pinocchio yelled, starting to cry again.

“I wouldn’t want to be digested either,” the Tuna added, “but I try to take things calmly, and I comfort myself by thinking that when you’re born a Tuna, there’s more honour in dying in water than in oil!…”
“Nonsense!” cried Pinocchio.
“That’s my opinion,” the Tuna replied, “and opinions, as Tuna politicians say, should be respected!”
“Anyway… I want to get out of here… I want to escape…”
“Escape, if you can!…”
“Is this Shark that swallowed us very big?” the puppet asked.
“Imagine: his body is more than a kilometre long, not counting the tail.”
While they were talking in the dark, Pinocchio thought he saw a kind of glow far, far away.
“What can that little light far away be?” said Pinocchio.
“It must be another of our unlucky companions, waiting, like us, to be digested!…”
“I want to go and find him. Couldn’t it be some old fish who can show me the way out?”
“I sincerely hope so, dear puppet.”
“Goodbye, Tuna.”
“Goodbye, puppet; and good luck.”
“Where will we meet again?…”
“Who knows?… Better not even think about it!”
chapters.title: Thrown into the sea, Pinocchio is eaten by fish and becomes a puppet again: but as he swims to safety, he is swallowed by the terrible Shark.

figures.alt: Pinocchio embraces Geppetto beside a candle inside the Shark.

paragraphs: As soon as Pinocchio had said goodbye to his good friend the Tuna, he began feeling his way through the darkness, and, groping inside the Shark’s body, he moved one step at a time towards the little light he could see flickering far, far away.
As he walked, he felt his feet splashing in a pool of greasy, slippery water, and that water smelled so strongly of fried fish that he felt as though he were in the middle of Lent.

The farther he went, the brighter and clearer the light became: until, after walking and walking, he finally arrived: and when he arrived… what did he find? You would never guess in a thousand tries: he found a little table laid for a meal, with a candle burning in a green glass bottle, and sitting at the table was a little old man, all white as if made of snow or whipped cream; he sat chewing small live fish, so very much alive that sometimes they even escaped from his mouth while he ate them.

At that sight, poor Pinocchio felt such enormous, unexpected joy that he almost went out of his mind. He wanted to laugh, he wanted to cry, he wanted to say a thousand things; instead, he made confused little sounds and stammered broken words that made no sense. At last he managed to let out a cry of joy, and, opening his arms wide and throwing them around the little old man’s neck, he began to shout:
“Oh, my dear Dad! I’ve found you at last! Now I’ll never leave you again, never again, never again!”
“So my eyes aren’t lying?” the little old man replied, rubbing them. “So you really are my dear Pinocchio?”
￼ch35

“Yes, yes! It’s me, really me! And you’ve already forgiven me, haven’t you? Oh, my dear Dad, how kind you are!… And to think that I, instead… Oh! But if you only knew how many disasters have fallen on my head and how many things have gone wrong! Just imagine, on the day you, poor Dad, sold your coat to buy me the alphabet book for school, I ran off to see the puppets, and the puppet master wanted to put me on the fire to cook his roast sheep, and he was the one who then gave me five gold coins to bring to you, but I met the Fox and the Cat, who took me to the Red Crayfish Inn, where they ate like wolves, and when I set out alone at night I met the murderers, who began chasing me, and I ran, and they followed, and I ran, and they kept following, and I ran, until they hanged me from a branch of the Great Oak, where the beautiful Little Girl with blue hair sent a little carriage for me, and when the doctors examined me they immediately said: ‘If he isn’t dead, it’s a sign he’s still alive’, and then I happened to tell a lie, and my nose began growing and wouldn’t fit through the bedroom door any more, which is why I went with the Fox and the Cat to bury the four gold coins, because I’d spent one at the inn, and the parrot began laughing, and instead of two thousand coins I found nothing at all, and when the Judge heard that I’d been robbed, he immediately had me put in prison to please the thieves, and when I came away from there I saw a beautiful bunch of grapes in a field, where I got caught in a trap, and the farmer firmly put a dog’s collar on me to make me guard the henhouse, and he recognised my innocence and let me go, and the snake with the smoking tail began to laugh and burst a vein in its chest, and so I went back to the beautiful Little Girl’s house, and she was dead, and the Pigeon saw me crying and said: ‘I’ve seen your dad building a little boat to come and look for you’, and I said: ‘Oh! If only I had wings too’, and he said: ‘Do you want to go to your dad?’ and I said: ‘Yes, please! But who’ll take me?’ and he said: ‘I’ll take you’, and I said: ‘How?’ and he said: ‘Climb onto my back’, and so we flew all night, and then in the morning all the fishermen looking out to sea said to me: ‘There’s a poor man in a little boat who’s about to drown’, and I recognised you from far away at once, because my heart told me it was you, and I waved for you to come back to the shore…”

“I recognised you too,” said Geppetto, “and I would gladly have come back to the shore: but how could I? The sea was rough, and a great wave overturned my little boat. Then a horrible Shark nearby saw me in the water and immediately rushed towards me, stuck out his tongue, scooped me up and swallowed me like a little stuffed pasta parcel from Bologna.”
“And how long have you been shut in here?” Pinocchio asked.
“Since that day, it must be almost two years now: two years, my Pinocchio… that have felt like two centuries!”
“And how have you managed to live? And where did you find the candle? And who gave you the matches to light it?”

“Now I’ll tell you everything. You must know that the very same storm that overturned my little boat also sank a merchant ship. All the sailors escaped, but the ship went to the bottom, and the same Shark, who had an excellent appetite that day, swallowed the ship after swallowing me…”
“What! He swallowed it in one mouthful?…” Pinocchio asked in amazement.

“In one mouthful: he spat out only the main mast, because it had stuck between his teeth like a fishbone. Luckily for me, that ship was loaded not only with meat kept in tins, but with ship’s biscuits, or toasted bread, bottles of wine, raisins, cheese, coffee, sugar, candles and boxes of wax matches. Thanks to all these gifts from God, I’ve managed to live for two years: but today I’m down to my last scraps: today there’s nothing left in the pantry, and this burning candle you see is the last candle I have…”
“And after that?”
“And after that, my dear, we’ll both be in the dark.”
“Then, my dear Dad,” said Pinocchio, “there’s no time to lose. We must think at once about escaping.”
“Escaping?… And how?”
“By getting out through the Shark’s mouth and jumping into the sea to swim.”
“That’s all very well: but I can’t swim, dear Pinocchio!”
“What does that matter?… You’ll climb onto my shoulders, and since I’m a good swimmer, I’ll carry you safely to the shore.”
“Dreams, my boy!” Geppetto replied, shaking his head and smiling sadly. “Do you really think a puppet barely a metre tall, like you, can be strong enough to swim with me on his shoulders?”
“Try it and you’ll see! Anyway, if it’s written in heaven that we must die, we’ll at least have the great comfort of dying in each other’s arms.”
Without another word, Pinocchio picked up the candle and, walking ahead to light the way, said to his father:
“Follow me, and don’t be afraid.”

And so they walked a long way, crossing the Shark’s entire body and stomach. But when they reached the beginning of the monster’s wide throat, they decided to stop, look around and choose the right moment to escape.

Now you must know that the Shark, being very old and suffering from asthma and a racing heart, had to sleep with his mouth open: so when Pinocchio reached the beginning of the throat and looked up, he could see a fine stretch of starry sky and beautiful moonlight outside that enormous open mouth.

“This is just the right moment to escape,” he whispered then, turning to his father. “The Shark’s sleeping like a dormouse: the sea is calm, and we can see as clearly as in daylight. Come along, then, Dad, follow me, and soon we’ll be safe.”

No sooner said than done, they climbed up the sea monster’s throat, and when they reached the huge mouth, they began tiptoeing along the tongue; a tongue so wide and long that it looked like a broad garden path. They were just about to make the great leap and jump into the sea to swim, when at that very moment the Shark sneezed, and as he sneezed he gave such a violent shake that Pinocchio and Geppetto bounced backwards and were flung down into the bottom of the monster’s stomach again.
The heavy fall put out the candle, and father and son were left in the dark.
“And now?…” asked Pinocchio, growing serious.
“Now, my boy, we’re completely lost.”
“Why lost? Give me your hand, Dad, and be careful not to slip!…”
“Where are you taking me?”
“We must try escaping again. Come with me, and don’t be afraid.”

With that, Pinocchio took his father by the hand: and still walking on tiptoe, they climbed up the monster’s throat together again: then they crossed the whole tongue and climbed over the three rows of teeth. But before making the great leap, the puppet said to his father:
“Climb onto my shoulders and hold me very, very tightly. I’ll take care of the rest.”

As soon as Geppetto was settled comfortably on his son’s shoulders, brave Pinocchio, sure of himself, jumped into the water and began to swim. The sea was as smooth as oil: the moon shone with all its brightness, and the Shark went on sleeping so deeply that not even a cannon shot would have woken him.
chapters.title: Inside the Shark, Pinocchio finds… who does he find? Read this chapter and you will know.

paragraphs: As Pinocchio swam quickly towards the shore, he noticed that his father, who was riding on his shoulders with his legs half in the water, was shaking all over, as though the poor man had a shivering fever.
Was he shaking from cold or fear? Who knows?… Perhaps a little of both. But Pinocchio, thinking he was trembling with fear, said to comfort him:
“Be brave, Dad! In a few minutes we’ll reach land and be safe.”

“But where is this blessed shore?” asked the little old man, growing more and more worried and narrowing his eyes like tailors threading a needle. “Here I am, looking in every direction, and I see nothing but sky and sea.”
“But I can see the shore too,” said the puppet. “Just so you know, I’m like a cat: I see better at night than in the daytime.”

Poor Pinocchio pretended to be cheerful: but really… really he was beginning to lose heart: his strength was fading, his breathing grew heavy and difficult… in short, he couldn’t go on, and the shore was still far away.
He swam as long as he had breath: then he turned his head towards Geppetto and said in broken words:
“Dad, help me… because I’m dying…”
And father and son were about to drown when they heard a voice like an out-of-tune guitar saying:
“Who’s dying?”
“Me and my poor dad!”
“I recognise that voice! You’re Pinocchio!…”
“That’s right; and you?”
“I’m the Tuna, your fellow prisoner inside the Shark.”
“And how did you escape?”
“I followed your example. You’re the one who showed me the way, and after you, I escaped too.”
“My dear Tuna, you’ve come just in time! I beg you, for the love you have for your little Tuna children, help us, or we’re lost.”
“Gladly and with all my heart. Both of you hold onto my tail and let me lead you. I’ll have you on shore in four minutes.”
As you can imagine, Geppetto and Pinocchio accepted at once; but instead of holding onto the tail, they decided it would be more comfortable to sit right on the Tuna’s back.
“Are we too heavy?” Pinocchio asked.
“Heavy? Not in the least: it feels as if I’ve got two seashells on my back,” replied the Tuna, who was so big and sturdy that he looked like a two-year-old calf.
When they reached the shore, Pinocchio jumped onto land first to help his father do the same: then he turned to the Tuna and said in a voice full of feeling:
“My friend, you’ve saved my dad! So I have no words to thank you enough! At least let me give you a kiss to show my everlasting gratitude!…”

The Tuna put his head out of the water, and Pinocchio knelt on the ground and gave him a very loving kiss on the mouth. At this sudden burst of deep affection, the poor Tuna, who wasn’t used to such things, felt so moved that, ashamed to be seen crying like a child, he put his head back underwater and disappeared.
Meanwhile day had come.
Then Pinocchio offered his arm to Geppetto, who barely had the strength to stand, and said:
“Lean on my arm, dear Dad, and let’s go. We’ll walk very, very slowly, like ants, and when we’re tired, we’ll rest along the way.”
“And where are we to go?” Geppetto asked.
“To find a house or a hut where someone will kindly give us a bite of bread and some straw for a bed.”
They hadn’t gone a hundred steps when they saw two ugly-looking creatures sitting by the roadside, holding themselves as if begging.

They were the Cat and the Fox: but they hardly looked like their old selves. Imagine, by always pretending to be blind, the Cat had ended up truly blind: and the Fox, grown old, mangy and weak down one side, no longer even had a tail. That’s right. That miserable little thief had fallen into such terrible poverty that one day he had been forced to sell even his beautiful tail to a travelling seller of small goods, who bought it to make himself a fly-whisk.
“Oh, Pinocchio!” the Fox cried in a whining voice. “Give a little charity to these two poor sick creatures!”
“Sick creatures!” repeated the Cat.
“Goodbye, you tricksters!” the puppet replied. “You fooled me once, and you won’t catch me again.”
“Believe us, Pinocchio, today we really are poor and miserable!”
“Really!” repeated the Cat.
“If you’re poor, you deserve it. Remember the saying: ‘Stolen money never bears fruit.’ Goodbye, you tricksters.”
“Have pity on us!…”
“On us!”
“Goodbye, you tricksters! Remember the saying: ‘The devil’s flour all turns to bran.’”
“Don’t abandon us!…”
“…us!” repeated the Cat.
“Goodbye, you tricksters! Remember the saying: ‘He who steals his neighbour’s cloak usually dies without a shirt.’”

With these words, Pinocchio and Geppetto quietly continued on their way; until, another hundred steps later, they saw at the end of a little path among the fields a pretty hut made of straw, with a roof covered in tiles and bricks.
“Someone must live in that hut,” said Pinocchio. “Let’s go and knock.”
And so they went and knocked at the door.
“Who’s there?” said a little voice inside.
“A poor father and a poor son, with no bread and no roof over our heads,” the puppet replied.
“Turn the key, and the door will open,” said the same little voice.
Pinocchio turned the key, and the door opened. As soon as they went in, they looked here and there but saw nobody.
“Where’s the owner of the hut?” Pinocchio asked in surprise.
“Here I am, up here!”
Father and son immediately looked up at the ceiling and saw the Talking Cricket on a little beam.
“Oh, my dear little Cricket,” said Pinocchio, greeting him politely.
“Now you call me ‘your dear little Cricket’, don’t you? But do you remember throwing a hammer handle at me to drive me out of your house?”
“You’re right, little Cricket! Drive me out too… throw a hammer handle at me too: but have pity on my poor dad…”

“I’ll have pity on both father and son! But I wanted to remind you of the rude way you treated me, to teach you that in this world we should be polite to everyone whenever we can, if we want to be treated with the same politeness when we’re in need.”
“You’re right, little Cricket, you’re quite right; and I’ll remember the lesson you’ve given me. But will you tell me how you managed to buy this lovely hut?”
“This hut was given to me yesterday by a pretty goat with a beautiful blue coat.”
“And where did the goat go?” Pinocchio asked, intensely curious.
“I don’t know.”
“And when will she come back?…”
“She’ll never come back. Yesterday she left, very sad, and as she bleated she seemed to say: ‘Poor Pinocchio!… Now I’ll never see him again!… The Shark must have eaten him by now!…’”
“Did she really say that?… Then it was her!… It was her!… It was my dear Fairy!…” Pinocchio began to cry out, sobbing and weeping bitterly.
When he’d had a good cry, he dried his eyes, made a comfortable little bed of straw and laid old Geppetto on it. Then he asked the Talking Cricket:
“Tell me, little Cricket, where could I find a glass of milk for my poor dad?”
“Three fields away from here lives Giangio the vegetable gardener, who keeps cows. Go to him, and you’ll find the milk you want.”
Pinocchio ran to Giangio the gardener’s house: but the gardener said:
“How much milk do you want?”
“A full glass.”
“A glass of milk costs one soldo. Start by giving me the soldo.”
“I haven’t even one centesimo,” Pinocchio replied, very ashamed and sad.
“That’s bad, my puppet,” the gardener replied. “If you haven’t even one centesimo, I haven’t even a drop of milk.”
“Never mind!” said Pinocchio, and made to leave.
“Wait a moment,” said Giangio. “You and I can come to an agreement. Would you be willing to turn the water wheel?”
“What’s the water wheel?”
“It’s that wooden machine used to draw water from the tank to water the vegetables.”
“I’ll try…”
“Then draw me a hundred buckets of water, and I’ll give you a glass of milk in return.”
“All right.”

Giangio led the puppet into the vegetable garden and showed him how to turn the water wheel. Pinocchio began work at once; but before he’d drawn a hundred buckets of water, he was dripping with sweat from head to foot. He had never done such hard work.
“Until now, I’ve made my little donkey do this hard work of turning the water wheel,” said the gardener; “but today the poor animal is close to death.”
“Will you take me to see him?” said Pinocchio.
“Gladly.”
As soon as Pinocchio entered the stable, he saw a fine little donkey lying on the straw, worn out by hunger and too much work. After looking at him very closely, he said to himself, disturbed:
“But I know that little donkey! His face isn’t new to me!”
And bending down beside him, he asked in donkey language:
“Who are you?”
At this question, the little donkey opened his dying eyes and answered, stammering in the same language:
“I’m Can…dle…wick.”
Then he closed his eyes again and died.
“Oh, poor Candlewick!” Pinocchio said quietly: and taking a handful of straw, he wiped away a tear running down his face.
“You’re so upset over a donkey that cost you nothing?” said the gardener. “Then what should I do, when I paid good money for him?”
“Well… he was a friend of mine…”
“Your friend?”
“A schoolmate of mine!…”
“What?!” Giangio shouted, bursting into laughter. “What?! You had donkeys as schoolmates?… I can imagine what fine studies you must have done!…”
Hurt by these words, the puppet didn’t answer: he took his glass of almost-warm milk and returned to the hut.

From that day on, for more than five months, he got up every morning before dawn to turn the water wheel and earn that glass of milk, which did so much good for his father’s weak health. Nor did he stop there: in his spare time, he also learned to make baskets and hampers from rushes: and with the money he earned, he very sensibly paid all their daily expenses. Among other things, he built a fine little cart himself to take his father out on pleasant days and let him get a breath of fresh air.

Then, staying up in the evenings, he practised reading and writing. In the nearby village, he had bought a thick book for a few centesimi, missing its title page and contents, and he used that to read. For writing, he used a little stick sharpened like a pen; and since he had neither inkwell nor ink, he dipped it into a small bottle filled with blackberry and cherry juice.
By doing his best to learn useful things, work and get on, he had not only managed to keep his still-sickly father almost comfortably, but had even put aside forty soldi to buy himself a new outfit.
One morning he said to his father:
“I’m going to the nearby market to buy myself a little jacket, a cap and a pair of shoes. When I come home,” he added, laughing, “I’ll be so well dressed you’ll mistake me for a great gentleman.”
And leaving the house, he began running, happy and cheerful. Then suddenly he heard his name called, and turning around, he saw a pretty Snail coming out of the hedge.
“Don’t you recognise me?” the Snail said.
“I think I do, and I think I don’t…”
“Don’t you remember the Snail who worked as a maid for the blue-haired Fairy? Don’t you remember the time I came down to bring you a light, and you had one foot stuck in the front door?”

“I remember everything,” Pinocchio cried; “tell me at once, lovely little Snail: where did you leave my kind Fairy? What’s she doing? Has she forgiven me? Does she still remember me? Does she still love me? Is she far from here? Could I go and see her?”
To all these questions, asked in a rush without stopping for breath, the Snail replied with her usual calm:
“My Pinocchio! The poor Fairy is lying in a hospital bed!…”
“In hospital?…”
“Sadly, yes. Struck by a thousand misfortunes, she has become very ill, and she no longer has enough to buy a bite of bread.”

“Really?… Oh, what sad news you’ve given me! Oh, poor dear Fairy! Poor dear Fairy! Poor dear Fairy! If I had a million, I’d run to bring it to her… But I have only forty soldi… here they are! I was just going to buy myself new clothes. Take them, Snail, and bring them to my kind Fairy at once.”
“And your new clothes?”

“What do I care about new clothes? I’d even sell these rags I’m wearing to help her! Go, Snail, and hurry! And come back here in two days, when I hope I’ll have a little more money to give you. Until now, I’ve worked to support my dad: from today on, I’ll work five hours more to support my dear mother too. Goodbye, Snail, and I’ll expect you in two days.”
The Snail, unlike her usual self, began running like a lizard in the blazing August sun.
When Pinocchio came home, his father asked:
“And your new clothes?”
“I couldn’t find any that fitted me well. Never mind!… I’ll buy them another time.”
That evening, instead of staying up until ten, Pinocchio stayed up until after midnight! And instead of making eight rush baskets, he made sixteen.
Then he went to bed and fell asleep. And as he slept, he seemed to see the Fairy in a dream, beautiful and smiling, and after kissing him she said:

“Well done, Pinocchio! Because of your kind heart, I forgive all the mischief you’ve done up to today. Children who lovingly care for their parents in poverty and illness always deserve great praise and love, even if they can’t be held up as examples of obedience and good behaviour. Be sensible in future, and you’ll be happy.”
At that point the dream ended, and Pinocchio woke with his eyes wide open.

Now imagine his amazement when, on waking, he realised he was no longer a wooden puppet: instead, he had become a boy like all the others. He looked around, and instead of the hut’s usual straw walls, he saw a pretty little room, simply furnished and decorated in an almost elegant way. Jumping out of bed, he found a lovely new outfit ready for him, a new cap and a pair of little leather boots, which fitted him beautifully.

As soon as he was dressed, he naturally put his hands in his pockets and took out a little ivory purse, on which these words were written: “The blue-haired Fairy returns the forty soldi to her dear Pinocchio, and thanks him very much for his kind heart.” When he opened the purse, instead of forty copper soldi, forty brand-new gold coins shone inside.

Then he went to look in the mirror, and he seemed to be someone else. He no longer saw the familiar reflection of the wooden puppet, but the lively, clever face of a handsome boy with brown hair, blue eyes and a look as cheerful and festive as a Pentecost celebration.
With all these wonders coming one after another, even Pinocchio no longer knew whether he was truly awake or still dreaming with his eyes open.

“And where’s my dad?” he suddenly cried; and going into the next room, he found old Geppetto healthy, lively and cheerful as before, having already returned to his work as a woodcarver and just then drawing a beautiful frame full of leaves, flowers and the little heads of different animals.
“Tell me something, Dad: how can you explain this sudden change?” Pinocchio asked, throwing his arms around his neck and covering him with kisses.
“This sudden change in our home is all thanks to you,” said Geppetto.
“Why thanks to me?”
“Because when boys become good instead of bad, they have the power to give even their families’ homes a new and happy look.”
“And where can the old wooden Pinocchio have hidden?”

“There he is!” Geppetto answered; and he pointed to a large puppet leaning against a chair, its head turned to one side, its arms hanging down and its legs crossed and bent in half, so that it seemed a miracle it stayed upright.
Pinocchio turned to look at it: and after looking for a little while, he said to himself with great satisfaction:
“How funny I was when I was a puppet! And how happy I am now to have become a good little boy!…”
chapters.title: At last Pinocchio stops being a puppet and becomes a boy.
